en: *Syādvādaratnākara*, verses 406–483:

Here it is said: "If omniscience is denied to the Enemy of Smara (Śiva) because he possesses defects, that is not correct; for this entire web of objections has already been addressed, as it remains [refuted] by what has been stated repeatedly. (356)

Furthermore, it is not fitting for those of mature intellect to deny the omniscience of Him who wears the moon upon his crest; for he alone is the eternal architect in the weaving of the thread of the three worlds. (357)

It cannot be argued by the clever that the threading together of the three worlds is unestablished, because it is established here through pure inference that transcends all other forms of inference. (358)
For instance:

"The subject of dispute has an intelligent cause because it is an effect; whatever is an effect here is so [i.e., has an intelligent cause], like a jar; and this [subject] is an effect, therefore it is considered so. (359)
First of all, no unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi) is observed in this proof, since the three categories of entities are indeed possible. (360)
Some things, such as mats, walls, and jars, have well-known makers; others, however, such as time and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), have no makers. || 361 ||
Certain [objects], such as the Kāśyapī mountain and others, have an uncertain author; these alone are designated here by the term "subject of dispute" (vivādapada) in this inference. (362)

Moreover, these [entities] are clearly established for cognizers by means of valid cognition; yet here, that which is called "being an effect" does not exist, and thus there is non-establishment even in terms of their own nature. (363)
For instance, certain things such as sprouts, rainbows, and lotuses are perceived directly by embodied beings as they are being born. (364)
In the case of mountains and the like, however, their status as effects is established by virtue of their possessing parts;
or else, it is established by their magnitude, or by their possession of motion, or by their possession of fluidity. (365)
For these very same reasons, those who are harsh in their logical investigations might attempt here to prove that there is an agent of the object under dispute. (366)
Because it is excluded from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) such as space, time,
and the quarters, the charge of inconclusiveness (vyabhicāritva) against the property of being an effect (kāryatva) here is not well-founded.
For this very reason, those rich in wisdom do not state "contradiction" as the intended meaning;
rather, it is "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa) that is here hinted at by the "glance of time. (368)
Because the proof of being an effect is stated immediately after the thesis (pakṣa), which is not sublated by perception, inference, or verbal testimony. (369)
Even the equality of its process, when being proclaimed, does not constitute a proof;
no inference here exists that could refute the opposing position. (370)
Furthermore, it is argued that Sthāṇu cannot possibly be the author of the dispute, because, being devoid of a body, he is like a liberated soul (muktātman). || 371 ||

Therefore, it is not the case that the subject (*dharmin*), Trilocana, is established by any means of valid cognition whatsoever; for by that very [means], the probandum (*sādhya*) here would be rendered inconsistent.
For this method of unimpeded creation of bodies and so forth would indeed be established;
and if that were established, what cause could appear to you, being pinned down by reality? (373)
Since this inference—free from all defects, highly proficient in refuting the notion of agency, and now fully awake—is present, we may now proceed without any anxiety. (374)

Is it not the case that here one intends to prove either merely that there is an intelligent cause, or a specific qualification of that? In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), for even our opponents accept the mere fact of an intelligent cause in the case of mountains and so forth; this is because the entire range of effects is born of karma, and karma itself has consciousness as its cause. In the second case, however, the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*). For instance, an omniscient intelligent being is intended here as the probandum (*sādhya*), yet in the example—the jar—that being is perceived as possessing characteristics entirely different from it. This is because [the conclusion] must follow the properties observed in the example.

Furthermore, since the cognition of an object already perceived occurs [in the case of a pot], the status of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is contradictory, because it establishes the opposite of the property one intends to prove. Moreover, the example is deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), because there is no such intelligent agent (*buddhimat*) in the case of a jar. Nor is it tenable to say that while the mere fact of having an intelligent cause is the subject of the proof, the specific quality of omniscience—which is not its subject—is nonetheless established from it.

For if that particularity is not the object of the proof, how can its establishment arise from it? If you say it is the object because it is already established, then how does it not touch upon the realization of defects residing in its own locus? That is incorrect; for even when there is pervasion by the mere universal, the universal—within which the particular is included—is inferred in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) by virtue of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference.

For instance, even the inference of fire does not have the mere generality of fire (*vahnisāmānya*) as its object, because that has already been established [prior to the inference]. Nor does it have the mountain qualified by that [generality] as its object; for since the generality of fire lacks a relation with the mountain, it cannot logically function as its qualifier. If a relation were admitted, then just as individual cows such as Śābaleya and others are "cows" due to the inherence (*samavāya*) of cowness (*gotva*), so too the mountain would have to be "fire" due to the inherence of fire-ness (*vahnitva*).

If it is argued that there is indeed a relation of "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) between the mountain and fire by virtue of the nature of fire, then this [relation] cannot be apprehended without first apprehending a specific fire conjoined with the mountain; thus, it would be the inference of that very specific fire. And in that case, the aforementioned fault would necessarily follow. This same [critique] should be shown to apply to the inference of the sense organ as well. For instance, even there, no action is observed to have the sense organ as its instrument; indeed, actions such as cutting and so forth do not have the sense organ as their means of accomplishment.

Because axes and the like are not sense organs, and because an action consisting of the discernment of color and so forth cannot possibly have an axe or similar tool as its instrument; therefore, just as in the case where the universal property of being an action (*kriyātva-sāmānya*), although pervaded by the general requirement of having an instrument (*karaṇamātra*), results in the establishment of a specific instrument characterized as a sense organ due to the presence of the property in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), so it is here as well.

Even though the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is pervaded by the mere presence of an intelligent cause, the establishment of a specific intelligent agent occurs through the force of its presence as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) in those things under dispute. Otherwise, even the general [cause] intended as the pervader would not be established, because that [general cause] cannot exist without specific attributes. Furthermore, it is impossible for one who is not omniscient to be the creator of the entire collection of effects such as mountains and sprouts, because such a person would lack knowledge of their material causes, instruments, recipients, and purposes.

For those who are the makers of something are necessarily cognizant of its material cause and so forth, as in the case of potters and the like. And since God is the maker of all effects, He must be cognizant of the material causes and so forth of all effects. Furthermore, the material causes in this context are the atoms of earth and the other elements.

The instruments (*upakaraṇa*) are merit and demerit (*dharmādharmau*), which reside collectively within the field (*kṣetra*). The recipients (*sampradāna*) are the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*), toward whom this [merit and demerit] leads by means of their own actions. The purpose (*prayojana*) is the experience of pleasure and pain for the knowers of the field. Therefore, although the scope of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists merely in having an intelligent cause, nevertheless, through the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), its specific nature is obtained; thus, the inference has a specific object as its domain. Nor does the aforementioned fault follow.

It might be argued that it is not mere "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) that is necessarily connected by way of essential nature (*svabhāvapratibaddha*) to having an intelligent cause; rather, it is a specific kind of effect. Upon seeing such a specific effect, the cognition that "it has been produced" arises even for one who has not observed an agent. And that specific effect arises only when it is seen to conform to the presence or absence of an intelligence. Such is the case with specific effects like jars and the like, but not with every effect in general, including the body, the world, and so forth; for in their case, no conformity to the presence or absence of that [intelligence] is observed.

Thus, by relying on the pervasion of having an intelligent cause (*buddhimaddhetukatva*) as induced by this specific limiting condition (*upādhi*), the general property of being an effect (*kāryatvasāmānya*) is not intrinsically connected (*svabhāvapratibaddha*) with that [intelligent cause]; therefore, it cannot lead to its inference. Otherwise, for one who relies on the pervasion of fire (*dhūmadhvaja*) as induced by smoke, there would follow the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of inferring the god of love (*makaraketana*) from paleness and so forth found even in water-lilies or pigeons. That [consequence] is outside the bounds of logic.

For there is no rule that every effect produces the cognition of an agent within itself, since such is not observed in the case of artificial gems and pearls, nor in the earth when it has been dug up and refilled. Furthermore, what is this specific quality of being an effect? Is it the conformity to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with an intelligent agent, or the observation thereof? If the former, that is already accepted by those who maintain that bodies, the world, and so forth have an intelligent cause.
For no one other than one possessed by a demon is capable of asserting that a cause does not conform to the presence and absence of its effect; this, however, is merely a [deluded] perception.

In that case, only that very cloth which was seen by him to follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of an intelligent agent is its effect, but not what exists in a different place. If it is argued that because something of that same class is seen to follow the positive and negative concomitance of that [agent], then anything of that class—even if its own positive and negative concomitance has not been observed—must likewise [be its effect], then why is the body, the world, and so forth not also considered such? If it is argued that only an effect belonging to the same class as a cloth is caused by an intelligent agent, [we reply:]...

[Objection: Surely a palace and the like would not have that [intelligent agent] as their cause, because they are of a different genus (*ajāti*) than cloth. [Response: Now, even though a palace and the like are of a different genus than cloth, they nonetheless possess a commonality with cloth due to some specific characteristic. If that is so, why should this not also apply to the body, the world, and so forth? Therefore, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*), which is intrinsically connected by its own nature (*svabhāvapratibaddha*), is established as having an intelligent agent as its cause.

And there is unity in the creator of earth and the other elements, because we observe the activity of multiple causal factors as being regulated by a single supervisor. We observe, for instance, that in the construction of a temple or similar work, the activity of numerous architects proceeds only when their operations are regulated by a single master builder. Furthermore, neither the eternity nor the uniformity of Trilocana and his cognition contradicts the occasional occurrence or the diversity of effects.

For the occasional nature and the diversity of effects are established through the occasional acquisition of various auxiliary causes. Now, if it is argued that the production of all effects, such as the body and so forth, will occur solely through merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) which have reached maturity at the appropriate time, what is the use of postulating a Lord (*īśvara*)? That too cannot withstand scrutiny; for since merit and demerit are insentient, they can never engage in their own effects without a conscious supervisor.

For it is thus: merit and demerit, being presided over by a conscious agent, proceed toward their own effects because they are insentient; whatever is such [is so] just as an axe is, and these two are likewise; therefore, it is so. Nor is our very self alone worthy of being postulated as the presiding agent of merit and demerit, because direct perception of it is impossible. Furthermore, the spontaneous activity of any insentient thing is not tenable; otherwise, it would continue to operate even once the effect has been accomplished.

Because [the Lord] is devoid of discrimination (*viveka*). Now, how does He preside over merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), given that these two reside only within the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*)? It is said: through a relationship (*sambandha*). For relationships are not limited solely to direct conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*); this is because "inherence in what is conjoined with what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyuktasamavāya*) is also a form of relationship. Indeed, the atoms that initiate the bodies and so forth of the individual souls are conjoined with the Lord; and through those [atoms], the individual souls and the merit and demerit inherent in them are likewise related [to Him].

Or rather, it is a conjunction through inherence (*samavāya*). This is because of the conjunction of the Lord with the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*), since an eternal conjunction is established through inference. For instance: the Lord is conjoined with the knowers of the field, because He possesses conjunction with corporeal substances; whatever possesses conjunction with corporeal substances is conjoined with the knowers of the field, just like a jar; and this [Lord] is likewise; therefore, He is so. Furthermore, this conjunction of His is eternal (*aja*), because of the absence of its causes—namely, conjunctions resulting from the action of either one of the two or from both.

Nor should it be argued: "How does the Lord impel atoms or merit and demerit that are themselves not supported by their own merit and demerit? For we observe that one who knows the science of poisons can impel poison even when it is not supported by his own merit or demerit. And there is a scriptural passage on this point: "The one God, creating heaven and earth, blows together with his arms and wings, he who has eyes on all sides, a face on all sides, arms on all sides, and feet on all sides" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.3).

Here, by the first attribute, omniscience is obtained, because seeing is indicated by the eye; by the second, the state of being a speaker, because speech is indicated by the mouth; by the third, the quality of assisting all, because assistance is indicated by the arm; and by the fourth, pervasiveness, because extension is indicated by the foot.

By the fifth [verse], he is the primary agent characterized by both dharma and adharma; for these two, by carrying out the course of the world, are like arms. By the sixth, he is intended as the primary cause in the form of atoms. For they are designated as "wings" (*patatra*) based on the etymology that they "fall" (*patanti*) due to their nature of moving through space. The connection with the prefix *sam-* in the word *saṃdhamati* involves a transposed preposition; thus, the meaning is either "he joins together" or "he produces. The term "the two heavens" (*dyāvā*) is an elliptical indication of the seven upper worlds, while "the earth" (*bhūmi*) refers to those below.

By the word "one" (eka), beginninglessness is indicated. Likewise: "Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; he sees without eyes, he hears without ears. He knows the universe, yet there is no knower of him; they call him the foremost, the Great Person."

Smṛti also states: "This ignorant creature is not its own master over pleasure and pain; impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or indeed into a pit" (Mahābhārata, Vanaparvan 30.28). And the words of Vyāsa: "There are these two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable. The perishable consists of all beings, while the unchanging is called the imperishable. But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Supreme Self—the immutable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.16; 15.18).
Therefore, there is indeed never at any time a single architect who threads together all the worlds, yet remains untouched by karma, afflictions, and the like.
Through his eternal knowledge, he has clearly understood the entire manifold of the universe;
thus, this conqueror of Tripura is established as such by means of a continuous series of arguments against [the notion of] birth.
O you who are like one utterly deluded, cast aside this falsehood and deceit;
is this a mere play to you, or is there some anger in your heart?
By which you cause even these believers, though they be experts in reasoning and practitioners of yoga, to be utterly deluded regarding their own true nature. 376.

[412] For thus, the followers of Yoga constantly seek to establish the faultlessness of liberation for Śiva; yet that [liberation] does not attain consistency, because here a contradiction between the two statements— namely, "constancy" and "liberation"— is difficult to reconcile.
He alone is truly liberated and renowned among the wise, for whom the process of bondage has been definitively overcome.
Indeed, just as a person here who has escaped from shackles that have themselves become loose is considered liberated. || 378 ||
And while bondage exists, how could there be, in any way whatsoever, the state of being endowed with eternity in liberation?
If that were so, then it would also be clear that the moon’s digit and the crest-lock [of hair] would always exist as effects. || 379 ||
O friend, since there is no such thing as its being destructible, why does its eternal existence even reach the level of a mere possibility?
O friend, since liberation itself does not exist for him, how could its permanence even come within the range of possibility? (380)
If liberation indeed exists for the beloved of Pārvatī, then by your own imagination, his state of being an effect also truly exists.
If, due to the absence of a cause, there is no state of being an effect, then let there be no liberation, because of the absence of the destruction of bondage. || 381 ||
Since he whose delusion has been destroyed holds the view that there is no creator, he is neither liberated nor bound.
Nor is he unliberated, since he does not possess the clinging of afflictions; therefore, by logical reasoning, he would be unliberated. || 382 ||
And he who alone is the supreme, eternal architect for the construction of the three worlds.
Even that infamy, "the lover of Kātyāyanī," does not bring you fame in this matter. (383)
For in that way, the construction of the three worlds would be possible for the one who bears the moon upon his crest.
Does activity proceed according to one's own will, or rather through dependence on karma?
Whether for the sake of dharma and so forth, or else out of playfulness and curiosity.
Either for the purpose of restraint or favor, or else for the arising of happiness. || 385 ||
Or else, for the purpose of dispelling suffering, or for the destruction of transgressions.
What need is there to mention the avoidance of future transgressions?
Is it from being filled with boundless compassion, or is it by its very nature?
These eleven types would thus be difficult for others to endure. || 387 ||
In the conceptualization of those from the East, the three worlds might sometimes appear even otherwise.
Indeed, there exists no fixed cause whatsoever for this partiality toward Virūpākṣa.
If he performs that [action] through the mechanism of karma, how could there be independence for him?
O friend, this is indeed independence for those whose activity always proceeds without dependence on others. (389)
Furthermore, it is certainly not logical for the Lord to engage in activity if his status as an agent depends upon karma.
For it is karma alone that will make the entire triple world a vessel for manifold ripenings.
An insentient thing does not perform an action here unless it is impelled by a conscious agent.
Just as the word "clay," when not set aside, is to be heard by those with ears standing before it. || 391 ||
How might the state of having accomplished one's purpose somehow come to pass for the Lord of Beings within the third eon?
The purpose of such a person as that, namely dharma and so forth, is destroyed and contradicted. || 392 ||
Moreover, Śambhu engages in the creation of the worlds out of a desire for play.
How then, my friend, could he be free from passion, like a circle of intoxicated children? (393)
Beholding the city, he thought: "This is the king, this is the queen, these are the charioteers, these are the galloping horses, and this is the herd of rutting elephants."
The neighboring kings bow down deeply out of fear; thus, even this multitude of children clearly finds delight on the banks of the Siprā river.
If Giriśa were to act for the sake of punishing or favoring others, then,
like such a worldly master, he would lack either dispassion or freedom from hatred.
Furthermore, such an activity of Śambhu does not lead to the arising of happiness, because you do not accept that happiness is an attribute [of God] in this context;
yet it has been accepted by those who maintain the doctrine of a Lord possessing ten attributes.
Alas, even by them he was approached as something truly eternal.
For him there is suffering and no happiness; likewise, for him there is never any transgression whatsoever.
Therefore, it is not logical for the leader of the Yoga school to assert a triad of distinctions such as suffering and the rest. (397)
He is completely filled by the overflowing nectar of merit and compassion.
The world proceeds in its creation; even that which is called "splendor" (bharga) is transitory.
For my dwelling is in some wretched village; in my home there is the seal of terrible poverty; my wife is hideous to behold; and I am the mother of daughters who are clever at harsh chatter.

Alas, for those beings who exist in this world, there is the state of being servants to a wicked master; if Śambhu creates such people who are consumed solely by suffering, then what kind of compassion could he possibly possess? (399)
Then, observing that dharma and adharma depend upon the ministers as their constituent parts in the performance of affairs;
Lord of the Mountain may bestow happiness or unhappiness here; yet that is inferior, because it is subject to subsequent negation.
This very nature of the wielder of the Pināka bow proceeds in the fashioning of the universe.
"It is incorrect to say that it is the very nature of the sun that it illuminates the worlds. (401)
For if the consciousness of God were thus rendered fruitless, then why should the process of setting the worlds in motion not proceed from their own inherent nature, even though they are insentient?

Therefore, they imagine for them [a creator]; why would these wise ones apply themselves to a useless entity such as Śiva? Is there ever any partiality on the part of the intelligent toward anything whatsoever? (402)
How could there be a purposeful activity in insentient worlds, restricted to specific locations?
Nor does the claim that there would be no cessation even when the effect has arisen enter the path of logical reasoning. (403)
Such erroneous conceptualizations arise solely from the reliance upon the doctrine of intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
There is no such consequence; otherwise, how could this [beauty] exist even on the crest of the moon, the bearer of nectar? (404)
Now, if you should say: "What is the use of these conceptual constructions? Let him act upon the three worlds in whatever way he pleases."
For its creator is well-established by the very fact that it is an effect, [and thus] free from the mire of the fault of falling away. || 405 ||
These words do not shine at all upon the minds of those possessed of intelligence.
It may somehow endure that which does not pass the touchstone of critical examination.

[415] For instance, what is this so-called "being an effect" (*kāryatva*)? Vyomaśiva says it is "inherence in the existence of its own causes. The meaning is that the relation—inherence—of an object such as a cloth with its own causes, which serve as its substrata (such as the threads), and with existence (*sattā*), which serves as its superstratum, is its being an effect. This does not strike one as clever; for since the definition of "being an effect" as you require is already indicated by the phrase "inherence in its own causes" alone, the inclusion of the word "existence" (*sattā*) is redundant.

For nothing that is non-existent can inhere in its own causes, because for that which is non-existent, its own causes do not even exist; furthermore, since inherence (samavāya) subsists in the five categories beginning with substance (dravya), there is nothing excluded by the term "existence" (sattā). If it is argued that this is a possible qualification, we reply: do we say that this is impossible? Rather, it is redundant. If one asserts that something is a definition merely by its existence, even if it is redundant, then far more would now have to be stated.

Now, as for the second definition of "being an effect," namely that it is inherence in existence (*sattā-samavāya*): this is not so. For it would be over-extensive, as it applies even to non-effects such as space (*ākāśa*) and the like, since [inherence in existence] occurs there as well. Alternatively, let "being an effect" simply be inherence in its own causes. But then, does that entity—such as a cloth—inhere in its causes while being existent, non-existent, both, or neither? If it is existent, does it exist by itself or through inherence in existence? If it exists by itself, what is the use of the operation of the cause?

Because this [existence] is eternal, like inherence (*samavāya*) and so forth which exist by themselves; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence that it never ceases its operation. Now, if it is argued that "it exists because of inherence in existence" (*sattā-samavāyāt*), we ask: does existence (*sattā*) inhere in that object while it is itself existent, non-existent, both, or neither? It cannot be the first position, because the object under dispute is not existent by itself; for if it were, it would follow that it is eternal, like inherence and so forth, and it would further entail the impossibility of its inherence in existence.

For indeed, that which exists by itself does not possess inherence, just as [inherence] does not exist in *sattā* (existence) itself. Yet, jars and the like are admitted to exist by themselves. Now, if it is argued that they are existent because of the inherence of *sattā*, then surely that inherence of *sattā* would also occur only in an entity that is already existent through another inherence of *sattā*; and that inherence of *sattā* would likewise exist only in that [entity] through yet another [inherence], and so on, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) through such repetition.

If it is argued that there are not more instances of inherence (*sattā-samavāya*) such that an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) might take hold, then let there be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). For the inherence of existence is established only when the existence of the entity is established, and the existence of the entity is established only when that inherence is established. Nor is the second alternative possible.

How could it not be like a cluster of manes on a non-existent elephant? For that [entity] is accepted as existing within the five categories of objects (*padārtha*), whereas what is non-existent lacks the status of being any one of those. Nor is the third [alternative] possible, because for proponents of monism (*ekāntavādin*), the acceptance of a dual nature—both existent and non-existent—is contradicted by their own principles. Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable, because the underlying intention here is this: "In its own nature, it is neither existent nor non-existent, but it is existent through its relation to existence (*sattā*). This is a flawed intention.

Because the negation of one is inseparable from the affirmation of the other. As for what Vyomaśiva says on this point, that is incorrect, because he accepts that the completion [of an action] and its connection [with the object] occur at the same time. For indeed, the production of entities is their very connection with their own causes, not their prior existence, since the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) has been refuted. And as for what Kandalī says: "In the case of impermanent things, however, existence (*sattā*) belongs only to that which was previously non-existent, due to the efficacy of the cause. Nor does this lead to the absurd consequence [of existence] applying to things like a donkey's horn."

The resolution [of this objection] is that no entity possesses the capacity for its own production. But even that is not a satisfactory solution for the wise; for in this way, one merely accepts the very position that inherence (*samavāya*) exists even when the thing itself does not exist, and the fault already mentioned applies there. Furthermore, it is subverted by both the *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) and its contrapositive: if the inherence of existence (*sattā-samavāya*) occurs in something non-existent, it follows that it must be existent, just like space (*vyoma*). Yet, the inherence of existence is admitted in effects such as cloth and the like. If, on the other hand, their existence is not desired, [then the premise is contradicted].

Let it be, then, that the opposite is the case, as with a sky-lotus; for cloth and other such things, which are the subject of dispute, do not exist. Nor is an effect existent [prior to production] by virtue of inherence in existence (*sattā-samavāya*), because if it were so, it would already inhere in its causes. Nor does it inhere there while being non-existent, because a non-existent thing, like a flower in the sky, cannot inhere anywhere. As for the two positions beginning with "having both forms," they are to be refuted in the same manner as the two preceding positions just refuted.

Furthermore, if being an effect (*kāryatva*) consists in inherence (*samavāya*) in its own causes, then it follows that inherence itself must be non-eternal, because it is occasional (*kādācitka*). If, on the other hand, this [inherence] is not occasional, then how could effects such as jars be occasional? For their defining characteristic—inherence in their own causes—would exist at all times. If you argue that it does not exist at all times, and that "being an effect" is said to consist in possessing the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of having the nature of a cause, and that when this [condition] is absent, it no longer possesses that condition; [we reply:]...

Just as when the staff is excluded, the person is not "staff-bearer"; nor should it be argued that in the absence of the adjunct (upādhi), the qualifier alone ceases to exist while the qualified entity remains exactly as it was.

"How could any logician proclaim that a qualified entity exists even in the absence of its qualifiers?"—all such speech is erroneous. For when the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in the form of the cause departs, is some part of the essential nature of inherence (*samavāya*) removed or not? If it is not, then since its essential nature remains exactly as it was, inherence would still possess its characteristic of being an effect even now, just as it did in the prior state.

If it is [the substance] that is removed, then its occasional nature is established by the removal of its very essence (*svarūpa*). Now, if "essence" is said to be its own property (*dharma*), then even if that distinct [property] is removed, not even a grain of husk of the substratum (*dharmin*)—namely, inherence (*samavāya*)—is destroyed. That is incorrect; for by the word "essence," we intend that very nature of this [substratum] which is its unique [characteristic] (*asādhāraṇa*) serving as the locus of all properties. And if that remains in its original state, [then nothing has been removed].

In that case, the same contingency as before would follow; otherwise, however, there would be occasional occurrence. Now, if the essential nature of a thing were to disappear even upon the removal of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of entirely distinct causes, then when a staff is released by a person, its essential nature too would have to vanish. This objection is like the instruction on a mouthful of nectar given by one who wishes to harm another. For it is indeed admitted that there is, in some sense, a disappearance of the essential nature, since the person, having first abandoned the transformation consisting of grasping the staff, assumes another transformation.

Furthermore, because there is no admission [of such a relation] in any way whatsoever, there can be no recognition [of identity] on the basis of its being a person (*puruṣa*). If it is argued that even in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), there might be such a loss of its own nature (*svarūpa-apagama*), then let occasional occurrence (*kādācitkatva*) also be like this. If that is accepted, then let impermanence (*anityatva*) also exist in some sense. If you say "Yes," oh, what a display of mere compliance (*vainayikatā*)! However, a potter who wishes to produce an effect such as a jar must first create inherence.

Since its being an effect consists in its inherence in its own cause, that [inherence] must first be established. Furthermore, since its being an effect would consist in another inherence in that [cause], that [second inherence] would have to be formulated first; thus there is an infinite regress. Consequently, "being an effect"—defined as the inherence of existence in its own cause—is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*). It is also partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*), because for yogis at the dissolution of all karma, there is an absence of both inherence and existence, due to their nature as absolute non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).

Now, if earth and so forth are made the subject (*pakṣa*) as being only positive entities by way of excluding non-existence (*abhāva*), then [the reason] is not unestablished in part (*bhāgāsiddha*). But how is non-existence excluded? Is it because this [world] has a non-intelligent cause, or because God is established even without making that [non-existence] the subject? If the first alternative is taken, then for those yogis who, while still alive, desire the union with the goddess of liberation—[it would follow that they too are created]. [518] For those who, while still living, desire some union with the goddess of liberation, which is equal to that of the yogis...
The worship of the two lotus-feet of the Moon-crested Lord would become useless. || 497 ||

Furthermore, dissolution likewise would not have an intelligent cause. In this way, it would be either causeless or have another [non-intelligent] cause. If dissolution were causeless, its eternal existence would follow, resulting in the adoption of the Śākya (Buddhist) view; or, by its eternal non-existence, there would be the eternal existence of all things. And thus, since even origination would be absent, how could there be any room for the postulation of an intelligent cause for the earth and so forth? The second position is also untenable.

Because the establishment of God is obstructed unless non-existence is taken as the subject [of the inference]: for if this intelligent creator were the maker of only a specific thing such as the earth, he would be a knower of only that much and not omniscient; thus, how could there be an establishment of God? If it is argued that his status as the creator of non-existence will be established through another inference, then the establishment of his omniscience does not follow from the inference based on the nature of being an effect (*kāryatva*). Nor do we perceive any other inference that serves as the basis for establishing his authorship of non-existence.

Therefore, the definition of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) as stated by Vyomaśiva—that its nature consists in the inherence (*samavāya*) of existence (*sattā*) in its own cause—is not tenable. Some maintain that "being an effect" is the inherence of existence in that which previously did not exist; this too should be understood as refuted by the very reasoning already mentioned. The author of the *Kiraṇāvalī* defines "being an effect" as "coming into being after having not existed. However, this is only possible when an agent is established who serves as the substratum for two distinct temporal actions, namely, the states of "not having been" and "having come to be," because this is the meaning of a sentence qualified by a word ending in the suffix *-ktvā*.

It is like the phrase "having heard, he reflects," where there is a single agent for both actions. However, in this case, there is no perception of an agent who serves as the substratum for both coming into being (*bhavana*) and ceasing to be (*abhavana*). Since the locus of non-existence does not exist while the locus of existence does exist, it is logically impossible for existence and non-existence to share a single substratum. Therefore, have you accepted that entities such as jars come into being after having already existed? If so, then you have sought refuge by entering the cage of the Sāṅkhya position, because you have resorted to the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).

That is incorrect. For us, it is easy to establish that something comes into being after not having existed, because there exists a single substratum for both its coming into being and its non-existence. Indeed, a jar exists in the form of a substance (*dravya*) while it does not exist in the form of a modification (*paryāya*); through contact with the potter, the wheel, the cloth, and so forth, it manifests in the form of a modification. And this is not the case in the system of Kapila; for in his view, causes merely bring about the manifestation of an entity that already exists in every respect, just as a jar obscured by a mass of darkness is revealed by the light of a lamp. [419]

Furthermore, if you accept our intended definition of "coming into being after not having existed" (*abhūtvā-bhāvitva*), it contradicts your own position. Consequently, your definition of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*)—as the nature of coming into being after not having existed—is unestablished in its own essence (*svarūpāsiddha*). Even if this were established in the case of things like clouds, trees, and bodies which are perceived after being unperceived, how could it be established in the case of mountains and the like?

If it is argued that there is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that Meru, the Makara, and so forth did not exist at all prior to their arising—such that the definition of "being an effect" (kāryatva) is unestablished in part because a total dissolution (*pralaya*) is unproven, and thus the proof of their prior non-existence is unestablished—we say: no. This is because a total dissolution is unproven. Furthermore, if you accept the proof of that [total dissolution] based on the proof of Śambhu [the Creator], then you fall into the fallacy of circular reasoning (*cakraka*).

For if Śambhu is established, the dissolution [of all things] is established in every respect; and when that [dissolution] exists, the establishment of the coming-into-being of Meru and other things—which previously did not exist—follows, and from that, the establishment of Śambhu follows. Furthermore, as for the proof of having parts (*sāvayavatva*) which was advanced to establish the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*), would that consist in inherence in parts (*avayava-samavāya*), conjunction of parts (*avayava-saṃyoga*), or non-separation from parts (*avayavāviṣvagbhāva*)? In the case of the position that it is inherence in parts, would "having parts" mean either having parts as its locus (*avayavādhikaraṇatva*) or having parts as its substratum (*avayavādheyatva*)?

In the first hypothesis, there is a lack of proof for both [the proponent and the opponent]; for neither the proponent nor the opponent accepts that parts are inherent (*samaveta*) in a whole. In the second hypothesis, however, there is an inconclusive argument (*anaikāntika*) due to the generality of "having parts" (*avayavatva-sāmānya*), which resides in the parts themselves; for although it exists therein, it is not an effect. Furthermore, as for what was said by someone to the effect that "it possesses parts because it exists together with its parts" on the strength of etymological derivation (*yoga-balena*), that too is untenable.

Our proof is not established because the specific property to be proven is unestablished; that is, the state of being composed of parts (*sāvayavatva*), which consists in the inherence of parts, is unestablished due to the non-acceptance of inherence. Furthermore, the position that it consists in the conjunction of parts is subject to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by virtue of space (*ākāśa*) and other such entities; for although objects such as jars possess the conjunction of parts, they are not effects [in the sense of being produced]. Nor should it be said that this [ether] lacks the conjunction of parts, for that would entail the consequence of its being non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). Pervasiveness consists in having the nature of being conjoined with all corporeal substances.

Nor is "having parts" (sāvayavatva) the state of having parts that are not distinct from [the whole], because that is unestablished for the proponent. As Udayana said: "Even though elsewhere 'having parts' is vitiated by such conceptual options, nevertheless, in this context, what is intended as 'having parts' is the state of being inherent in a different substance."

Even in that case, when the word "composite" (*sāvayava*) is used in its general sense as "that which exists together with parts," how does it acquire this specific meaning—that for a substance, being composite consists in its inherence in another substance? For although, in order to establish the non-eternality of sound, one might employ the reason "knowability" (*prameyatva*), and even though "knowability" is defined as being an object of valid cognition, nevertheless, in this context, the intended meaning is understood to be its occurrence only in non-eternal objects such as cloth; thus, a specific distinction is obtained.

Alternatively, since the inherence (*samavāya*) [of one substance in another] is not established even if it were somehow obtained, the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*)—defined as the state of being inherent in another substance within a substance—is also unestablished (*asiddha*). As for the proof (*sādhana*) that was stated, namely "because of possessing action while having magnitude" (*mahattve sati kriyāvattvāt*), therein the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddhi*). This is because magnitude is absent in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), which is included within the subject (*pakṣa*). Nor should it be said that the dyad was not made the subject; for if that were so, it would follow that the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is likewise unestablished in that case.

And it is not the case that even in the fundamental inference (*mūlānumāna*) there is no inclusion of that [dual atom] as the subject (*pakṣa*); this is the essential point. For in that case, without a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), how could its exclusion from the subject be determined? For a dispute is indeed "contradictory discourse" (*viruddhavāda*) where such a dispute is reported. And contradictory discourse certainly exists even regarding the dual atom (*dvyaṇuka*). For you say, "The dual atom has an intelligent cause," while we say otherwise. Now, if the subject is formulated with a qualification, namely, "the dispute concerning something other than the dual atom," then [the fault is avoided].

In that case, there is another alternative. Furthermore, how can the fact that a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) has an intelligent cause be established in this way? And if that is not established, how can the omniscience of anyone be established? [For] no one knows that a dyad has a non-intelligent cause. If it is argued: "Whoever produces something must necessarily know its material cause and so forth; thus, once it is established that a dyad has an intelligent cause, it follows as a matter of course that there is knowledge even of the dyad which serves as that material cause, and likewise, omniscience is also established. [Response: ...

That too is not sound. Even so, omniscience remains unestablished. For if the fact that a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) has an intelligent cause is not established, then ignorance alone persists regarding its constituent material causes (*upādāna*). And if that is the case, how can omniscience be proven? Furthermore, if atoms are unknown to anyone, how could a dyad be produced? Indeed, it is your own position that atoms, presided over by Īśvara, initiate the dyad. But presiding over things that are unknown is impossible.
And when the dyad (dvyaṇuka) became unfit for the vow, the three worlds fell into a state of great distress.
Or rather, what is surprising here: that an improper act leads to misfortune? || 408 ||
And thus, O most excellent ones, O foremost in yoga, the accomplishment of Śiva has been achieved by you through this measure.
If you should say that another proof is required for the establishment of the effect-nature of the dyad (dvyaṇuka), [then listen].
Then, in that case, you would hear the contradiction while it is still present.

As for what was stated regarding "possessing a structure" (*racanāvattva*), that too is not tenable. For what is this so-called "structure"? Is it the possession of various locations (*pradeśa*) or the conjunction of parts (*avayava-saṃyoga*)? If the first alternative is held, then there is an inconclusive argument (*anaikāntika*) with respect to space (*antarikṣa*). This is because those locations, which are the basis for the conjunction of all corporeal substances, exist there as well. Nor should it be said that they [the locations] are merely metaphorical in that case; for if that were so, it would follow that space could not produce the actions of all corporeal things.

Even its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is not desirable [in this case], because it would depend on an unseen auxiliary (*adṛṣṭa-upakāra*) that is distinct from the nature of the space (*nabhodeśa*) which is merely metaphorical (*upacarita*). For it is impossible for an unseen factor to provide assistance to a metaphorical ear—which, being non-existent in nature, is like a eunuch (*vāndhyeya*). Now, suppose the second alternative [is held]: what then is the relationship? Is it having that [conjunction] as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), or is it inherence in the same object (*ekārthasamavāya*)? If the first, then it is unestablished for the opponent (*prativādyasiddhi*). Indeed, the status of the conjunction of parts as a non-inherent cause is not established for us.

Inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), however, is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*). For, by virtue of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), even non-effects such as universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth inhere in a single object—namely, the form of a constituent part (*avayava*)—just like the parts themselves. You should understand that this [inherence] has been refuted by the inference that will be stated later regarding the refutation of the universal "being an effect" (*kāryatva*). By this, that which was asserted—that some agent is established by these very same reasons—is also discarded.

[Objection: But if these inferences have been thus refuted by you, is it not established that mountains and the like possess the property of being effects (*kāryatva*)? If that were so, they would be eternal. [Reply: It is said: That very point is indeed accepted here; however, we say that these inferences do not establish the proof of *kāryatva*. If it is asked, "Then how is the proof of the probandum (*sādhya*) achieved through these inferences? [we reply: Not even from what is established for both parties.

Because this [inference] is subject to the fallacy of doubtful deviation (*sandigdhavyabhicāritva*) due to the absence of a means for apprehending the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). If it is argued that perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) are indeed the causes for apprehending that [connection] only when it is extremely well-known, then—since you accept the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) only within a domain suitable for perception and non-perception—let there be a certain deviation established by grass, trees, lightning, and so forth, which are beyond the reach of human activity. If you argue that "grass and such are not included in the subject (*pakṣa*), and therefore there is no deviation from what is included in the subject," do not say so.

Because there is no logical justification for making that which is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) the subject of a thesis (*pakṣa*). Otherwise, even in cases such as "fire is not hot because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*), the mere act of making it the subject would have to be the refuge.

Furthermore, if one were to raise an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of the very subject under consideration (*pakṣīkṛta*), it would follow that the seal of all inference (*anumāna*) is broken. For it could indeed be said even regarding the inference of smoke: "Smoke deviates from fire on the mountain slope, because it exists there even without it. If fire had been directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) there as well, who indeed would not acknowledge such deviation? But this is not the case.

Because perception is blunted—due to its presence in an unsuitable location—with respect to both affirmation and negation therein, there arises doubt. It is for this very reason that there is occasion for a logical reason (*hetu*), according to the maxim: "The statement of a reason applies when there is doubt. But such [doubt] does not exist in the present case. For even by those standing nearby, who are attentive and one-pointed in mind, there is no non-perception of grass and the like through direct perception; indeed, it is direct perception itself that is called "non-perception" with respect to a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) in relation to another counter-correlate.

Therefore, what is actually sublated by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is said to be sublated by inference (*anumāna*) only with respect to the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). And when something is sublated by inference, there is no room for another inference [to apply]. Now, if it is argued that [the opponent] intends to establish the absence of an intelligent agent (*buddhimat*) specifically as a "visible" entity—since intelligence is common to both visible and invisible things, and thus the restriction of its visibility is untenable—how can there be a negation of an intelligent agent in the production of grass and such things based on mere non-apprehension? If it is then argued that, because of this doubt, it is proper to take it as the subject of the thesis (*pakṣīkaraṇa*), [we reply:]...

This is quite extraordinary. For, by the very fact that perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) are granted authority to establish pervasion (*vyāpti*), the acceptance of "visibility" (*d�rśyatā*) follows as a necessary consequence. Indeed, neither perception can serve as the means to establish positive concomitance (*anvaya*) regarding an invisible object, nor can non-perception serve as the means to establish negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Yet, one whose mind is terrified by the deviation [of inference] caused by grass and the like might nevertheless grasp a pervasion with an intelligent agent who is beyond the scope of perception, while [the grass] is clearly observed.

One may accept this, but for him, the recourse to perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) in that regard is not superior. [Objection: Is it not the case that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*) occurs through mere rationality (*prekṣāvattva*) alone, without depending on the qualification of being "visible" or "invisible"? [Reply: It is not so. For even by that much, there is simply no room for a pervasion established by perception. Indeed, how could that [pervasion], which is restricted to things whose nature is exclusively visible, have as its object a form common to both the visible and the invisible?

For that visible and invisible form, although it follows the same properties such as being apprehended by a single cognition, belongs to entirely distinct classes due to the remoteness or proximity of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, perception—which functions by accepting only the visible class and is ignorant of all else—indicates only that specific [visible] universal property as the pervader (*vyāpaka*), even though it is common [to both]. Although that which is remote in space and time is not visible, it nevertheless belongs to the same class by virtue of its fitness for perception.

Because that which is remote by its very nature is excluded by perception itself. For if all other things were excluded, the inference would terminate in a restricted particular, and thus there would be no pervasion (*vyāpti*) at all. Just as the pervasion established by perception—which functions by taking as its primary object a burning, radiant form suitable for its own operation—is not restricted to a common form shared with the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) when it concerns the seven-rayed fire (*saptārcis*).

Otherwise, even regarding a form that is intended [to be perceived], one who doubts—just as in the case of the distinction between grass fires (*tārṇa*) and so forth—would not engage with single-pointed cognition to obtain the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by it. Or, for example, the pervasion established by perception when a breeze causes leaves to flutter does not terminate in a form common to still air, because it prioritizes a tangible form. Otherwise, if one were to infer the wind from the shaking of sprouts, one would certainly not perform actions of engagement or withdrawal in accordance with a wind possessing a specific tangible quality.

Likewise, even for an intelligent person, a pervasion established through perception does not terminate in a form that is common to both the visible and the invisible. Therefore, if by the pretext of perception one asserts that mere valid cognition (*pramiti*) alone constitutes the establishment of pervasion, then that certainty regarding causality produced by perception would terminate in a form that encompasses both the visible and the invisible. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is a certainty of causality produced by perception does not terminate in a form that encompasses both the visible and the invisible.

Just as in the case of fire, [the argument] that "this [fire], having abandoned its common form produced by the stomach, is perceived" constitutes the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). For being restricted to a perceptible or imperceptible form is pervaded by the state of not being perceived; and since the determination of a cause as being perceived is incompatible with that, the pervasion exists. Thus, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) possesses a doubtful exclusion from the heterologue (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva*).

Furthermore, if one intends to express a pervasion (vyāpti) by means of smoke alone, setting aside the qualification of being "visible" or "invisible," then when a proponent demonstrates the absence of the potter's effect in the absence of an intelligent agent (*buddhimad-abhāve*) in order to establish negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the absence of mere consciousness (*cetana-mātra*) devoid of the qualifications of being visible or invisible established? This is because the non-perception of the visible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) has jurisdiction only over the negation of that which is visible; otherwise, it would be impossible to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to [the presence of] grass and the like.

For non-perception directed only toward a perceptible person cannot be established as a means for proving the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of mere intelligence; this is because the absolute difference in their objects is evident. Otherwise, why would non-perception directed only toward a perceptible person not also serve to confirm the deviation of "being an effect" [from "having an intelligent agent"] in the case of the production of grass and the like? For by that same [non-perception], it would be possible to negate even an imperceptible agent in those cases as well. Indeed, there is no such maxim as "entry upon gaining [the object] and exit upon cutting [it]."

Therefore, since there is no means of apprehending the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) when the specific qualification of the visible object is excluded, the reason remains under-extended (*avyāpti*), and thus doubt persists regarding its exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Nor is the observation of the absence of both [the probandum and the reason] in space the means for apprehending the negative concomitance; for it is impossible to ascertain that the absence of "being an effect" is necessitated by the absence of "operation by an intelligent agent. Indeed, only when all other causes are present can the absence of an effect—occurring solely upon the absence of that [specific cause]—be understood as being necessitated by that absence.

But the mere absence [of activity] is easily established for both cause and effect according to the analogy of the female slave and the donkey. And thus, there arises a doubt: is the absence of "effectness" in the sky due to the absence of the operation of an intelligent cause, or rather due to the mere absence of any cause? In that case, such an effort is futile. For even regarding positive concomitance (*anvaya*), there remains a doubt as to whether it is to be grasped between the mere effect and the mere cause, or rather between the effect and a cause qualified by a person (*puruṣa*).

Now, if this particularity, which consists in the nature of a specific person as the cause, is indeed perceived—just as the nature of fire is perceived in smoke—how can it be set aside? If that is so, and the particularity consisting in a visible body is indeed apprehended—just as the radiant form of the sun is—how can it be set aside? If you argue: "That particularity is indeed subject to deviation (*vyabhicārin*), because we observe 'effectness' (*kāryatva*) in things such as mountains even without a maker possessing a visible body," [we reply: Let it be subject to deviation.

However, just as you assert a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) based on the cause being a qualification of a specific person because it has been observed, so too should a positive concomitance be asserted only for an effect that has been previously observed—such as an ancient palace—and not for [an effect like] a mountain; what is there to prevent us? [Objection: But if this were so, how could the Jains ever establish supersensible entities through inference? [Reply: That is not correct.

For those who maintain that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) arises from inference based on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of perception and non-perception, such defects cannot possibly arise. However, for those who maintain that its apprehension occurs through perception and non-perception alone, there is no liberation from those defects. Furthermore, how could the apprehension of the pervasion of "mere effect" by way of a specific intelligent cause be consistent with perception and non-perception?

For these two—perception and non-perception—proceed precisely by delineating specific types of cause and effect in order to grasp the causal relationship. Thus, immediately following the operation of perception and non-perception, one observes: "From such a thing, characterized by a blazing and radiant nature, there arises a substance that produces such an alteration in the throat of a fly, which is as grey as the neck of a pigeon."

From such a specific person, there arises [an effect] with a shape characterized by a broad base and belly; however, from that [other cause], there arises [an effect] consisting of threads arranged as warp and woof. By means of this form, the causal relationship proceeds by delineating two distinct classes [of causes and effects], thereby excluding all other types of cause-and-effect categories.

This very same course applies everywhere in the cognition of the relationship between cause and effect; it is certain that this statement transgresses the established method because of its adherence to [the doctrine of] God (*īśvara*). Now, you might say: "What, then, is this 'adherence' here? If perception were to apprehend the pervasion of the mere effect by the intelligent agent—setting aside distinctions such as mountains and so forth, just as one perceives the pervasion of mere smoke by fire, setting aside distinctions such as grass-fed fires and so forth.

In that case, just as for those who follow the external [Buddhist] view, the apprehension of pervasion occurs by including within it merely a subtle sub-class of the class of effects, namely smoke; so too let it be for the intelligent [creator] as well—[the apprehension of pervasion] should be of a specific class of effects such as cloth and the like, but not of effect in general.

Or, just as you seek to grasp the pervasion of the mere effect by subsuming even utterly dissimilar classes [of things], why do you not likewise grasp that same pervasion through fire—namely, "wherever there is a mere effect, there is fire"? How could the external operation of the sensory perception itself adopt two different modes of activity in these two cases?

If it is argued that this distinction is based on the observation and non-observation of deviation—namely, that while mere effects deviate from fire (*citrabhānu*), they do not deviate from an intelligent agent—then such observation and non-observation, unless they have ascended to the level of reflective inquiry (*vimarśa*), are like the touch of grass underfoot by one who is walking and are thus useless for practical discourse (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, there must necessarily be a corresponding reflective inquiry; yet such an inquiry does not exist here.

Indeed, when the perception and non-perception that grasp positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding fire, smoke, and so forth have not occurred, one does not experience the conceptual construction that "the entire class of effects arises from fire"; rather, through the observation of repeated deviation—since other effects are perceived even in the absence of fire—one determines the certainty that "only smoke is produced by this [fire]."

However, immediately after perception and non-perception, one determines that from this fire and so forth comes this smoke and so forth, identifying two specific universals as being in a cause-and-effect relationship. Furthermore, does this observation of deviation undermine inference only when pervasion (*vyāpti*) actually exists? It cannot be the first position, because of contradiction; for it is impossible for there to be both pervasion—characterized by the logical reason’s inseparable connection with the probandum—and the absence of inference caused by the possibility of the probandum’s absence.

In the second case as well, does that [subsequent cognition] establish the falsity of the pervasion while the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) grasping the pervasion is already manifesting by its own power, or does it bring about the destruction of the validity of that very same [first cognition]? In the former alternative, the refutation is exactly the same as before. In the latter, however, does it bring about the destruction of its validity in all instances involving inferential objects, or only in specific ones?

In the manner previously described, even the inference of fire from smoke might not exist. What, then, will remain as a refuge for the inference of God? Even regarding a restricted object, does the observation of deviation—by virtue of one's own desire or because of one's own activity therein—cause the loss of validity for the means of knowledge that grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*)? If, by virtue of one's desire, the observation of deviation remains indifferent toward the establishment of pervasion in a restricted object, then in reality there is no such thing as a "reason" (*hetu*) or a "non-reason" (*ahetu*).

For even in the case of smoke, there would be the undesirable consequence of the pervasion being undermined by one's own whim. However, since activity occurs only toward that very [object], how can perception—which has a restricted object—have as its domain even that which is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? To this it is replied: just as the perception grasping pervasion is held to have all things as its object because it possesses a cognition that functions toward a restricted genus (i.e., it grasps "being an effect" in general), so too let that which has deviation as its domain also have all things as its object. How then could it have a restricted object? Because both have objects that are neither less nor more.

Therefore, since the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) concern one and the same object, how could there still be a means of proof (*sādhana*) or a non-means of proof? Let it be granted, out of deference to you, that the observation of deviation has a restricted object; nevertheless, the cognition of that [deviation] in those things possessing deviation does not occur all at once, but rather sequentially. Furthermore, at the time of grasping the pervasion, there is no direct observation of deviation even among those things that do deviate. Thus, because smoke lacks any distinction from effects such as cloth, it would follow that it is not a [valid] reason (*ahetu*).

Or else, if smoke were the cause, it would follow that cloth and other effects would also be its causes. Nor should it be argued that because deviation is observed in all other effects, the certainty of pervasion (*vyāpti*) rests solely in the case of smoke; for this point is impossible to establish, since the objects of potential deviation are infinite, and a human lifespan is too short compared to the time required to investigate those things remote in space and so forth. Therefore, just like the observation of deviation, the apprehension of pervasion is also faultless only when restricted to a specific domain.

If it is argued that, in this way, when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been grasped by one person, the establishment of the "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) fallacy becomes untenable because another person points out an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), we reply: this is indeed so, provided there were a restriction on the sharpness of everyone's intellect.

However, a person of dull intellect, even though perception has occurred regarding a specific class (*jāti*) through similarity and other means, unifies it with a different class and, out of the conceit of having grasped the pervasion, persists in relying upon inference. When another person of sharp intellect demonstrates the deviation, he is made to realize that the pervasion is difficult to grasp.

Therefore, the establishment of the inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) is common [to both]. For example, even when smoke has appeared, one who recalls an object as pervasive with fire—grey like the throats of pigeons—as being grasped by the cognition of pervasion, might infer fire from a mass of dust blown up by the wind; yet, having pointed out the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) caused by the rising of steam, he is dissuaded due to the lack of expertise among those well-versed in the matter. Consequently, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) must be understood through perception as being restricted solely to specific types (*jāti-viśeṣa*). Now, if the cognition is indeed restricted to specific types...

In that case, how could these cloths and so forth—possessing the refinement of substances such as turmeric because they are associated with color—lead to the inference of the refinement of substances like turmeric in the case of "like a previously perceived cloth," and so on? For how could things such as cloths and mats, which are of an entirely different genus (*atyantavijātīya*), indicate the refinement by substances like turmeric merely through their association with color? Or, if they were to lead to such an inference, then why would even entirely heterogeneous things like Mount Kailāsa and the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*) not likewise infer a Person (*puruṣa*), since they too possess the common property of being effects? [To this we reply: It is not so.

Because here it is the effect, as the pervaded (*vyāpya*), that serves as the indicator (*gamaka*), and because it is only with respect to that [effect] that one must consider whether something is of the same class (*sajātīya*) or of a different class (*vijātīya*). And that [pervasion] is twofold—depending on whether the object is something to be produced (*nirvartya*) or something to be modified (*vikārya*)—namely, in due order, consisting of the substratum (*dharmirūpa*) and consisting of the attribute (*dharmarūpa*). Among these, when there is an absolute production of what was previously non-existent, the pervasion of the substratum is stated, as in the case of smoke and so forth. For in that case, only another instance of smoke is "of the same class," while any other thing is "of a different class."

But when there is the arising of another property in that very same thing which was previously situated, then pervasion (*vyāpti*) is said to exist, as in the case of heat and so forth in water. And in that case, it is simply another instance of heat that constitutes the homogeneous property (*sajātīyo dharmaḥ*); there is no longer any requirement for the identity of the substratum (*dharmijāti*). For instance, in the inference "this water is conjoined with fire because it is hot, like ghee," the homogeneity belongs only to the two properties called "heat" as they reside in the water and the ghee; it does not belong to the two substrata, the water and the ghee.

In the same way, redness (*rāga*) also, disregarding the heterogeneous nature of substances such as cloth or *kaṭā* [wool], indicates the refinement of a substance solely by virtue of its being of the same genus as its own essential nature. For this very reason, when there is a particularity in that [redness], a refinement caused by saffron in one case or turmeric and so forth in another is inferred. And it is not the case that, in the instance of pre-existing mountains, clouds, and the like, an agent is desired merely as one who brings about their "effect-ness" (*kāryatvamātra*); rather, he is like a potter and others, one who produces them anew.

Therefore, the apprehension of the pervasion of the factual subject (*dharmivastu*) does not depend on the proximity of the mere property (*dharma*); nor is the pervasion of the property the homogeneity of the subject. Consequently, even when there is a difference in kind (*vaijātya*) of the subject—as in the case of passion—the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) does not function as a prover. Otherwise, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of inferring fire from a white substance would be difficult to avoid.

Because the response based on deviation has already been refuted, the cognition of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) by perception is therefore restricted solely to specific types of effects. And if perception, even though it operates upon the distinction between types of effects, were to take "effect" in general as its objective basis, then why should it—operating upon an effect—determine only a "cause" in general as its pervader? Why does it instead rely specifically on that which has the nature of an intelligent agent (*buddhimat*)?

Therefore, if there is no concession to your position, this perception must apprehend both [the general and the particular]—either by apprehending the universal (*sāmānya*) or by apprehending the particular (*viśeṣa*). If it apprehends the universal, what can be said regarding the establishment of Virūpākṣa through the inference of a cause in general from an effect? And if it apprehends the particular, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established by means of the mere effect. Consequently, it is established that perception, based on experience and reasoning, demonstrates a specific class of effects as being pervaded by a specific cause.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever perception apprehends a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) possesses a function restricted to a specific class (*viśiṣṭajāti*). For example, [the perception] of fire and smoke. And this [perception] which establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the effect by an intelligent agent is likewise. There is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to the suspicion of its functioning otherwise, because that is sublated by the non-perception of a cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*). For indeed, a difference in causes is the cause of a difference in effects; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that everything would be without a cause. Furthermore, a difference in causes is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

This is because [the cognition] arises from a common causal complex characterized by the object, the sense faculty, light, and so forth. Furthermore, should there be a suspicion that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhya*), one must state the subverting argument (*bādhaka*): whatever is perceptual has a function restricted to a specific genus, as in the case of the cognition grasping deviation; and the perception grasping the causal relation between fire and smoke is likewise perceptual. Here too, the same resolution of the inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) applies.

And thus, because the various classes of effects are infinitely diverse and mutually distinct, and because one must apprehend the pervasion (*vyāpti*) for each specific class of effect, it is inconsistent to claim that inference is valid only so long as every type of effect has been determined to be preceded by an intelligent agent; this is indeed inconsistent. If it is asked, "What kind of class of effect is pervaded by an intelligent agent? it is said: that upon seeing which, even one who has never observed the actual process of production, forms the cognition that it was made.

[Query: Is that [cognition] the cognition of the means of proof (*sādhana*), or rather the cognition of the subject under discussion (*prakṛtasādhya*)? First, as for the cognition of the means of proof, it is already established for you, since earth and the other elements are accepted as being effects. Now, let us consider the latter position. In that case, the meaning would be this: "This 'effectness' perceived in earth and the others is not capable of inferring the probandum (*sādhya*), but is something else entirely, because it does not generate the cognition of the probandum. But this is not tenable.

Because this would entail the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference (*sarvānumānocchedaprasaṅga*). For even in the case of smoke and the like, one could just as well say: "This smoke is not capable of inferring fire; rather, it is something else entirely, because it does not produce the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*). And thus, the means of proof (*sādhana*) is not established as long as the cognition of the probandum is not established, and the probandum is not established as long as the cognition of the means of proof is not established; therefore, the mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is quite evident. [The opponent replies: That is not satisfactory.

Since "one whose intellect is fixed" (kṛtabuddhi) does not mean one whose intellect is directed toward the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), nor even one whose intellect is directed toward the subject of proof under discussion (*prakṛtasādhya*), but rather one whose intellect is directed toward the object of accomplishment that is the very nature of the weaver and so forth; and because of that absence, neither the non-establishment of your reason (*hetu*) nor the non-establishment of the subject of proof under discussion is intended to be stated directly. Rather, this is a demonstration of absolute heterogeneity (*atyantavaijātya*). By means of that, the non-establishment or the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the reason is precisely what is intended.

For instance, the cognition of a craftsman arises with respect to a temple or similar structure seen in an empty city, but not with respect to Mount Malaya, the ocean, and so forth.
