The intention is that the presence or absence of this cognition of craftsmanship does not occur without an absolute difference in genus (*jāti*). Therefore, just as the cognition of fire arising from smoke, while not arising from a donkey or the like, necessarily establishes a difference in genus between smoke and the donkey.

In the same way, this [inferential cognition] also [arises] from entities whose human origin is certain, such as Mount Kailāsa or the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*). If it is asked, "How then is the absence of identity with the producer to be understood here?"—[the answer is: because there is not even a suspicion in a dream that a weaver or the like could be the source of the ocean or the thunderbolt; otherwise, the world would be beset by the misery of droughts resulting from the trampling of the weaver's feet.

Or, one who is terrified by the invasion of a foreign army might seek refuge beyond the barrier of mountains and oceans, and thus find cessation from that very threat. If you argue that for you as well, another [cause] standing in the place of a weaver must be expected, we say: no. If the effect belongs to the same genus [as its cause], it is illogical to search for a cause of a different genus; for the accomplishment of the goal is achieved by the weaver alone. Indeed, even in the case of another cloth, there is no expectation of anything other than the weaver. If you argue that in the case of a specific type of garment, there is an expectation of a specialized artisan, [we reply: so be it.

However, as long as there is a firm conceptual identification (*parāmarśa*) of a common nature through the medium of a cloth, for that very reason, it is the conceptualization of the weaver himself, the craftsman. But in the absence of such a conceptual identification, there is doubt regarding its being of human origin. Mountains such as Meru and Mandara, however, are not objects of a single conceptual identification by anyone as being of human origin.

Therefore, by denying the extreme heterogeneity of these things—which is established by direct perception—one must accept that very same [heterogeneity], because otherwise it would follow that there could be no inference of a common artisan between one cloth and another. For just as in the case of mountains and the like, which belong to the same genus as garments and other objects, an agent distinct from weavers and the like is inferred, so too, in the case of another garment whose production has not been witnessed by weavers and others, one would not infer a weaver or similar agent.

But this is not the case. Therefore, it is established that mountains and the like do not possess the same generic nature (*sajātīyatva*) as jars and the like. Since the specific kind of effect such as a jar is invariably connected with a person (*puruṣapratibaddha*), whereas the effects such as embryos and infants are not of that same kind, the specific property of being an effect (*kāryatvaviśeṣa*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*) in that case. Furthermore, since the kind of effect such as an embryo or infant is not pervaded by a person, the mere property of being an effect (*kāryatvamātra*) lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*). This being the case, the objections—which function by preventing the arising of the cognition of the probandum under discussion—are cast far aside.

For we do not claim that the reason "being an effect" (kāryatva) is unestablished because of the absence of a cognition [of an agent] regarding the specific probandum under discussion. What then? We claim that because there is an absence of a cognition of an agent such as a weaver in the case of Mount Mandara and so forth, the property of being an effect belonging to the same class as cloth and the like is unestablished in those cases; and consequently, there is no fault whatsoever in the fact that there is a lack of the cognition of an agent for the specific probandum at hand. Furthermore, if it is accepted that the mere state of being an effect—on the grounds of its observation in things such as pots—is the inferential indicator of an intelligent cause in the case of mountains and the like;

In that case, why should the fact of being a modification of clay (*mṛdvikāratā*) on Indra’s head not likewise lead to the inference of a human creator? For here too, the state of being a modification of clay does not differ between a jar and an anthill; nor is such a specific configuration impossible for a human to produce. If it is argued that, despite its similarity, it is not the effect of that [human] because one does not observe its following the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [human], we say no, for the same logic applies here as well.

In this case as well, let it be that everything which conforms to the presence of an intelligent being is preceded by such a being, as is the case with palaces and the like. However, it cannot be so for the world and similar entities, because they lack conformity to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of such an agent.

[Objection: But if this is so, let every particular instance of smoke whose presence and absence are observed to follow the presence and absence of fire be preceded by fire; however, how can fire be inferred from [smoke] located on a mountain slope, since that [particular smoke] is not the object of a cognition of the universal? If you argue that this is because the determination of the absence of a cause is the same here as well, then why should the peak of Indra’s head also be considered such [i.e., a product of human effort], simply because walls and other things have been observed to be products of humans?

If it is argued that this is not the case because a certain particularity arises from walls and such things, as in the case of Śakra’s head and so forth, then that particularity must also arise from palaces and the like, as well as from the world and so forth; thus there is no distinction. However, there is no such essential difference between smoke-particles that follow the positive and negative concomitance of fire and a smoke-particle located on a mountain.

For this very reason, one cannot infer fire from mere white substance, such as a water-lily or a pigeon; for it is only the universal "smokeness" that serves to differentiate [the specific smoke] from those. Furthermore, if you maintain that even the earth and other elements possess the nature of being effects because you observe that the mere property of being an effect follows the positive and negative concomitance with an intelligent agent in the case of jars and the like, then it would follow that gems, pearls, and so forth—which are observed to follow the positive and negative concomitance with human agency—must also be effects of that [human agent], even when they arise from jewel-mines.

If it is argued that even in those cases, a person is indeed accepted as the creator, then how is it that the world’s usage of the term "unauthored" (akṛtrima) regarding them is of an unerring nature? If you say it is because a creator such as Īśvara is not perceived there due to being beyond the senses, we say no; for in all other cases as well, a creator is not perceived, since it is impossible to perceive a creator who is remote in space or time. Therefore, the usage of the term "unauthored" applies to those [scriptures] as well, insofar as their creators are unseen.

Alternatively, there may be a commonality of purpose with things such as those arising from the ocean, because there is no distinction [between them]. If it is argued that the term "artificial" is applied because an agent is observed among things of that same class, and thus an agent is inferred even for those whose makers are not seen; then why should the term "artificial" not also apply to things of the sea, since they too are of the same class as those whose makers are observed? Otherwise, let it not apply here either, as there is no difference between the two cases.

In the case of oceanic phenomena, since they are of a different genus from artifacts such as gems whose makers are observed, it is possible to infer a maker; however, in the absence of the conventional designation "artificial," there would likewise be no inference of a maker for effects such as stationary objects, because they too are of a different genus from artifacts like palaces whose makers are observed. Since there is no distinction [between the two cases], there could be no inference of a maker. Therefore, it is only logical to infer a maker for those things that are of the same genus as artifacts with observed makers, such as rivers, streams, and mountains, because neither ordinary people nor investigators conceive of them as being artificially produced.

Thus, it is established that such a specific "effect-ness" (kāryatva) is unproven in the case of the earth and other such things; furthermore, mere "effect-ness" lacks a proven pervasion (vyāpti). As for the rejection of the charge of "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa) fallacy on the grounds that the subject (pakṣa) is not sublated by perception and other means of knowledge—that too is not clear. For even a portion of the subject, such as grass and the like, which possesses a creator capable of being perceived, is nonetheless perceived as lacking a perceived creator, and is thus sublated by perception.

Now, if it is argued that a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśa*) cannot be sublated here by perception because an agent is incapable of being apprehended through perception, we say: no. For it has already been stated that since the grasping of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is accepted as occurring through both perception and non-perception, the formulation of the proof must necessarily apply only to an object that is perceptible.

Moreover, the self (ātman), which possesses knowledge, desire to act, and effort, is indeed a corporeal agent, because potters and others are observed to be so. And such an agent is certainly capable of being apprehended through perception. Even though the aspect consisting of knowledge and the rest is not [itself] perceptible, nevertheless, because the corporeal aspect—which is perceptible—is negated, this constitutes a sublation of [the opponent's] perception. Alternatively, it might be argued that only that which possesses knowledge, desire to act, and effort is called an "agent," and not that which possesses a body as well.

[Objection: Why does the body not participate in the state of being an agent? [Reply: If you say it is because it is employed for the production of knowledge, then let knowledge also be abandoned, since it is employed for desire. Let desire also be abandoned, since it is employed for effort. Consequently, one arrives at the conclusion that the agent is merely that which possesses effort. Thus, alas! The Yogas have perceived this most desirable agency and have declared that the agent is not conscious. Therefore, the agent must be said to possess the fourfold set beginning with knowledge.

And thus, there is a perceptual sublation [of the opponent's position]. Now, the body is not included as part of the agent, because it is exhausted in other functions. However, there is no agency without cognition; for in this context, cognition is not merely useful for desire. Rather, it is also useful for delimiting the object of desire and effort. For desire and effort do not themselves incline toward their own objects; rather, they possess their objectivity only by means of the delimitation of the object provided by cognition.

If the determination of the object were due to the intrinsic nature of those two [desire and effort], it would follow that cognition is denied. For this indeed is the distinction of cognition from them: that it is by its very nature directed toward the object. Therefore, it is not proper to discard cognition merely because it lacks utility elsewhere, since desire and effort have a further utility for the sake of determining the object. Consequently, the agent is precisely the substratum of cognition, desire, and effort; the body, however, is merely useful for cognition and thus does not constitute the locus of agency.

If this were the case, perception would be a subverting proof [of the opponent's position], because it is impossible to perceive through direct observation an agent who is the substratum of the triad beginning with cognition. This is incorrect; for it is reasonable to say that in the case of someone like us, whose desire and effort are impermanent, there must first be a determination of the object, and once that has been determined, having ascertained its nature as a means to pleasure or pain, desire and effort proceed accordingly.

Furthermore, for one for whom these two are eternal, since they are established by themselves wherever they may be, they exist through their own nature; what, then, would be the use of knowledge? For those two do not proceed preceded by knowledge, as that would entail the contradiction of their eternality. But was it not said that if desire and effort were directed toward delimiting an object by themselves, they would possess the nature of knowledge?

That is incorrect. For what is the meaning of "delimitation by an object" (*viṣayāvaccheda*)? Does it mean cognition (*jñapti*) or activity (*pravṛtti*) with respect to a specific object? In the former case, those two would be of the nature of knowledge; however, we do not accept that position. But in the second case, how could these two be of the nature of knowledge? Nor should it be argued that activity itself would be impossible for them without the cognition of an object, because since those two are eternal, they are always active toward any object whatsoever, just as dimension (*parimāṇa*) is [always present] in space (*vyoman*).

Now, although these two [desire and effort] are eternal, they do not have only a single object, because it is possible for them to have various objects depending on the conditioning factors (upadhāna) of this or that particular entity. Thus, in whatever entity serves as a conditioning factor when cognition arises, desire and effort come to have that very thing as their object, just like the light of the sun. Without cognition, it would be difficult to establish for those two their status as having such-and-such an object. As it has been said: "Since a conditioning factor cannot possibly exist by means of an entity that has already arisen, there would otherwise be the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya)."

For indeed, it is only when an entity has already arisen that, given its presence (*upadhāna*), desire and effort take that entity as their object; and conversely, it is only when desire and effort have arisen that there is the presence of the entity. Now, since we observe [beings] only in conjunction with bodies, let us assume that [the case of God] is also like that. Or, if it is accepted that his knowledge, desire, and effort exist even without being accompanied by a body, because they are distinct from the knowledge, desire, and effort of beings such as ourselves; [then the following applies].

In that case, since their desire and effort are distinct from the desire and effort of people like us, let the accompaniment of knowledge also be abandoned; for among inclinations, only those directed toward beloved objects deserve respect. Furthermore, if knowledge is sought merely to delimit the object, then let it be sought; but what is the use of desire? For the object of effort is already delimited by knowledge alone. Nor should it be argued: "How can effort proceed without desire?"

Because that [agent] is eternal, it would always be active wherever [the effect occurs]. If one imagines a desire for vision elsewhere, then one must also imagine a body. If it is argued: "Let there be a body, but let it be invisible; thus, since it is not seen in grass and such things, the reason is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed)," [we reply]: But why is this possessor of a body invisible? Is it due to the power of spells (*vidyā*) and so forth, or due to a particular class of being (*jāti-viśeṣa*)? If the power of spells and so forth were the cause of invisibility, he might be visible at some time. Indeed, perpetual invisibility is not possible for those who possess the power of spells, tantras, and the like.

For it is only at the very time of the application of the injunctions and so forth that its invisibility is possible; moreover, the claim that a specific genus (*jāti*) is the cause of its visibility is also unworldly.

Because a specific genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*) is impossible for a single [individual], since that [genus] resides in multiple individuals. For in the case of *piśācas* and the like, there are indeed multiple individuals; thus, it is logical that their invisibility results from a specific genus. However, since no such [genus] is perceived in the case of an agent possessing a visible body—such as grass and so forth—it is established that [the reason] is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). Furthermore, as for what was stated regarding the inference presented as the basis for pointing out a "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) argument—namely, that by some means of valid cognition [it is known that] Trilocana and so forth [are the authors]—that too is untenable.

In this case, the subject (*dharmin*) is established by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). How a subject can be established even by conceptual construction will be demonstrated later. Alternatively, let it be that this subject is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); in that case, it is impossible to establish the charge that the reason is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). For if its establishment were asserted through some means, such as the skill in creating mountains and so forth, then it would be subject to the critique under discussion.

To the extent that it is said that the proof [of the Lord] arises from the grace of the Blessed One’s scriptures, it should not be argued that this proves him to be the creator of those [scriptures]. For he is described therein specifically as a particular *khecara* (sky-farer), possessed of the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇiman* and endowed with extreme power; there is no mention whatsoever of his being the creator of the earth and other elements. Now, if it is argued that such a proof establishes [only] a specific type of *vidyādhara*, we ourselves accept that such a being is not the creator of the earth and so forth.

But there is no contradiction with that [subject] which we intend. Do not say so. For that very Śiva who is accepted by you as possessing the excellence of omniscience and so forth is, for us, simply a particular *vidyādhara*; he is not anyone other than that. Therefore, even though there is disagreement regarding the specific qualities, it is entirely appropriate for Śambhu to be the subject (*dharmin*) in a general sense. In all other cases as well, the subject is always stated in a general sense; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the collapse of inference itself.

For it could indeed be asked, even regarding the inference of the non-eternality of sound: "Is this sound a substance, a quality, all-pervading, or otherwise; and is that which is being heard the subject (*dharmin*) or something else? Therefore, because the subject is stated in a general sense, there is no fallacy of "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). Now, if the relationship of pervader and pervaded were established such that "whoever is an agent is embodied," then the presence of a body in God would subvert his agency as well. But this is not the case.

The agency of the body is not established as a pervading property, because the connection with a body is conditioned by the non-eternality of the agent's intellect; for it is only an agent whose intellect is non-eternal that requires a connection with a body, and no other.

That is incorrect. For what is the definition of a limiting condition (*upādhi*)? If you say it is "that which does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*) while having co-extensive pervasion with the probandum (*sādhya*)," then that [condition] certainly cannot even enter the realm of possibility regarding the agent's connection with a body. For just as a body does not pervade the agent, so too does the non-eternality of cognition. Furthermore, you yourself have stated that a limiting condition is not something that pervades the probans.

Otherwise, even the connection with wet fuel would be an *upādhi* for smoke in relation to its connection with fire; for like fire, that [wet fuel] too would pervade the probans, which is smoke. Therefore, because of the possibility of such an *upādhi*, the body's pervasion of the agent is not established. Now, this might be so if the non-eternality of the intellect were a pervader of the agent; but it is not so. For whatever is intellect is necessarily eternal, since the connection with non-eternality in respect to the intellect is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*).

Likewise, since there is no agency even where the absence of impermanence in cognition exists—given that the notion of permanence can arise in some cases—how could that [notion] be the pervader of impermanence? The connection between the cognition of an adjunct (*upādhi*) and impermanence is a co-inherence in a single object not previously perceived. For it is precisely that cognition which is impermanent, insofar as it inheres together with the unperceived [impermanence] in a single locus such as ourselves. That, however, is not sound.

Because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the inherence in a single object with the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and the non-eternality of cognition, it cannot be adduced as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Indeed, the transformation of food such as vegetables is not called a "limiting adjunct" when it lacks pervasion with blackness. Furthermore, one must state that the absence of pervasion does not exist here in the case of liberated souls (*muktātman*); for such a form of liberation will be refuted later. Or, even if such a form of liberation were to exist, the inherence in a single object with the unseen merit would still not be a limiting adjunct, because it is itself non-eternal.

Furthermore, since being pervaded by the probans (*sādhanavyāpakatva*)—like damp fuel (*ārdrendhana*) and so forth—is not a qualifying condition (*upādhi*), [your argument fails]. Now, suppose it is argued that the conjunction with the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭasamavāya*) is caused by defects; therefore, cognition is impermanent only where there is a conjunction with the unseen in a defective substratum, whereas in a different, defectless substratum, cognition will exist but the conjunction with the unseen will not. But surely, you have not accepted a defectless substratum for the liberated soul (*mukta-ātman*), nor have you admitted the existence of cognition therein.

However, the faultlessness of God is not yet established. Therefore, because the conditions (upādhis) stated by you are untenable, it is proven that the agent possesses a pervasive body. As for what the author of the *Kandalī* said: "Is agency merely the state of having a body, or is it the status of being the employer of causal factors whose efficacy is observed? Agency is certainly not merely the state of having a body, because that would entail the consequence of agency for one who is fast asleep or indifferent.

Rather, [the cause of action] is the status of being the employer of causal factors whose efficacy has been observed; for when that exists, the production of the effect occurs. And this [status] is possible even for one who is bodiless, just as it is for the self (*ātman*) in the case of impelling its own body. If it is argued: "In that case too, he possesses that very [body] acquired through his own karma," we reply: True, he possesses it; however, it does not serve as the means for impelling [another], because of the contradiction of an action directed toward oneself. If it is argued: "[The body] exists as the object to be impelled," [we reply: Then for the Lord (*īśvara*) as well, there exists an atom (*paramāṇu*) to be impelled. That too is not tenable.

For we define agency as the possession of a body, knowledge, volition, and effort acquired through one's own karma. In the states of deep sleep or neutrality, however, although the mere body exists, there is no production [of action] because of the absence of knowledge, desire, and effort directed toward the intended effect. Furthermore, even one who performs an action characterized by the impelling of one's own body is necessarily connected to a body acquired through his own karma; so where is there any scope for the charge of deviation? Nor is there any contradiction regarding an action operating upon itself.

For even in the case of propulsion, there is no contradiction in the body itself being the means, just as there is no destruction anywhere of the whole that possesses parts. Furthermore, the absence of contradiction here should be addressed in the same way as the self-luminosity of knowledge was previously established. By this, that which was said by someone is also refuted: "Does the body have a direct operation toward the effect, or an indirect one? Not the first alternative, because of deviation; for when a yogi brings forth serpents and the like through the power of yoga, the body does not have a direct operation at that time."

Now, as for the second [objection]: even if God is the agent, there is still bodily activity by way of a causal series. For even God, when initiating a multitude of effects, depends upon the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) residing in individual souls (*kṣetrajña*). And since that [unseen merit] arises in a self delimited by a body, there is thus bodily activity here too by way of a causal series.

Since it is established that the body of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) does not belong to the Lord as something acquired through his own karma—whereas a body acquired through one's own karma is pervasive of agency—and since that [type of body] is absent in Rudra, there is an absence of agency in him; for this reason as well, there is an "equal-to-the-point-under-discussion" (prakaraṇasama) fallacy here in the inference. The subject of dispute is not caused by an intelligent agent, because it does not produce pleasure and pain for an agent. Whatever is caused by an intelligent agent necessarily produces pleasure and pain for an agent, just like a pot. But this [the world] is not like that.

Therefore, it is not caused by an intelligent agent. Furthermore, regarding the doubt as to whether what is intended to be proven here is merely the state of having an intelligent cause or a specific [agent], it was stated at the conclusion of that inquiry that the specific nature of that agent is obtained through the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

That too is incorrect. For the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) demonstrates merely the exclusion of non-connection with the subject for that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), since this is exactly what is observed in cases such as the inference from smoke. Otherwise, just as there is the exclusion of non-connection with the mountain cave for fire based on smoke, there would follow the undesirable consequence of inferring that the fire possesses a mass of five-colored flames. If you argue that there is no such capacity [in the reason], then it follows that the capacity resides solely in the exclusion of non-connection with the subject.

In this case as well, let there be the establishment of the mere exclusion of non-connection with the subject (*pakṣāyogavyavacchedamātra*) by the force of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). But how could an eternal cognition as the agent be established? For it is not the case that because a mountain and so forth are effects, they must therefore have an eternal cognition as their cause. If it is argued: "It follows; since agency by a mere intelligent being is untenable, [the fact of being an effect] implies an eternal cognition as its own agent," then this is simply the grace of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Otherwise, inference based on what has been inferred (*anumitānumāna*) would be abolished.

And that [existence] is not undesired. For, having established that desire and the rest possess an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) on the grounds that they are qualities (*guṇatvāt*), one proves through the inference of elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*) the existence of a specific substance in the form of the Self (*ātman*), which is distinct from the eight [known] substances. Furthermore, according to the view of those who maintain that the Lord possesses six attributes, a specific presiding agent is established by virtue of the property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*): namely, Śiva (Kapālī), who possesses only eternal consciousness regarding all objects.

Those who maintain that the Lord possesses eight qualities cannot accept this. They argue that the entire range of cosmic effects cannot arise through mere knowledge of the material cause and so forth. Indeed, even a potter who knows the material cause and the like is never capable of beginning the production of a jar if he does not desire to make it, or if he desires it but fails to exert himself due to laziness regarding those materials and so forth. Therefore, the production of an effect arises from the combination of knowledge, desire to act, and effort; it cannot come about from knowledge alone.

Indeed, smoke produced by the burning of wet fuel does not arise from wet fuel alone, nor from fire alone. Suppose it were so in the case of the cognitions of ordinary persons; however, the cognition of the Blessed One is of a different nature, and thus it is sufficient for every effect in the universe even without assistance—if this is your argument, then alas! what is the use of his cognition at all? His own essential excellence (*svarūpātiśaya*) alone will suffice for each respective effect. If you argue that no effect whatsoever arises from a single, unassisted cause, [we reply: [This is not the case].

[Objection: But surely merit and demerit reside in the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and atoms exist as his auxiliaries; so what is the use of this knowledge? [Reply: If it is argued that they do not operate unless known, and therefore such knowledge must be sought—then why do they not operate once they have been cognized?

If it is argued that [the creator] is not perceived in such ways through means such as a jar and so forth, then one must likewise accept both the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and the effort (*prayatna*), just as one accepts knowledge. Furthermore, in that case, knowledge is directly employed for a specific desire to act, and that [desire] is [employed] for a particular kind of effort; thus, since effort alone is the direct cause for the production of the effect, how could that [production] be possible without it?

For indeed, rice does not succeed merely from the friction of a great mass of wood without fire, nor merely from the wind of hissing breath flashing from the hollows of a *vaṭa* tree; therefore, let God be established as the substratum of the eight qualities. To this we reply: that too is not well-founded, because his will and effort must be either eternal or non-eternal. If they are eternal, then what is the use of God’s knowledge, which would be useless for producing desire-to-create (*cikīrṣā*) and effort? For since those two [will and effort] are non-eternal, they do not depend on anything else for their own production.

Furthermore, his knowledge, unlike his effort, is not a factor for the production of the effect that is direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). Indeed, when there is a difference in effort, he presides over the material cause and so forth in that very same way; however, at that time, no utility whatsoever belongs to his knowledge or to his desire to act (*cikīrṣā*). For an instrument that does not produce any distinction in an action whose performance is already accomplished lacks the status of being an instrument. Thus, the omniscience of God is dismissed with a final salutation. And this has already been stated previously. Now, suppose those two [knowledge and desire] were impermanent.

In that case, the cause of their production must be stated. If it is argued: "But surely eternal cognition itself is the fundamental cause of production; so what need is there for another cause?"—alas, what a lapse! For he has now resolved to assert that desire and effort—which have the specific contact between the self and the mind as their non-inherent cause—arise from mere cognition alone even in the absence of those two. If that were so, he would indeed be able to produce rice without even using rice-grains!

If it is argued that there certainly exist conjunctions of this [Self] with liberated souls and minds, and therefore, assisted by them, this [Self] produces simultaneously in various places the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and effort (*prayatna*) for the sake of generating those effects—[we reply: Are the minds and their conjunctions uncontrolled (*anadhiṣṭhita*) when they produce the desire to act and effort, or are they controlled (*adhiṣṭhita*)? If they are uncontrolled, then there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason "being an effect" (from the property of being produced by a conscious agent) due to these very two, namely, the desire to act and the effort.

But presiding over [the body] is indeed impossible without effort. That presiding occurs through another effort, which arises from a further desire to act (*cikīrṣā*). And there is no infinite regress, because this stream of desire to act and effort is accepted [as beginningless]. If this is argued:

Now, one might object: "When this Lord, desiring to withdraw the world, remains inactive for some time while the collections of merit and demerit in the individual souls (kṣetrajña) have their functions suspended and the universe has reached the state of atoms, and then, when He desires to act and exerts effort—since no prior desire or effort exists to produce the desire and effort that are to be generated—how can there be the presiding over the minds and their conjunctions? If this is the objection:

Desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and effort (*prayatna*) would not arise from the mind and its conjunctions if they were not presided over [by a conscious agent]; or, if they were to arise [without such a presiding agent], how could they not contradict the reason [of their] being effects? Furthermore, it has been stated that the body is also pervaded by an agent; and since he does not possess such a body, how could he be an agent?

Śaṅkara maintains that his body certainly exists. Now, is it eternal or non-eternal? If it is eternal, is it partless or with parts? It cannot, first of all, be partless; for it would have to be either one of the eternal substances such as the atoms of earth or an independent entity. Yet it is not independent, because that would entail the reduction of the total number of substances. Furthermore, even if it were one of the eternal substances such as the atoms of earth, it would have to be either all-pervasive or non-pervasive.

It is not all-pervasive, because that would contradict its being presided over by a Lord (*īśvara*). Nor is the mind (*manas*) [the body], since it is restricted to being connected with a specific self. Furthermore, how can its nature as consisting of atoms of earth and so forth be determined? For there exists no derivative substance (*kāryadravya*) such as earth and so on that is composed of those [atoms]. Nor is that body possessed of parts (*sāvayava*), because that which has parts is incompatible with permanence. Nor is it impermanent; for is it caused by an intelligent agent (*buddhimaddhetuka*), or otherwise? It cannot be the latter.

For this would result in the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*), since [the world] could be caused by an intelligent agent who is either another creator or one's own creator. If it were caused by another, then the same question would recur: is that other creator embodied or bodiless, and so forth? In that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite number of gods (*īśvara*). Now, you might say: "Let this be a festival for us! For even a single Blessed Lord was difficult to find; how then can their infinity be attained now? This too is the speech of one who sees only the surface.

For there would be the consequence that the activities of many beings with conflicting intentions could not produce effects such as the earth; or else, even if produced, there would result an inconsistency due to the influence of a manifold God. Even if he were his own creator, does he create that body while being embodied or while being unembodied? If he is unembodied, then let the Lord likewise create the three worlds while remaining unembodied. If he is embodied, then in order to produce that body, he must first fashion another body for himself.

To bring that [body] about as well, another body must first be created, and thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, since its power would be exhausted solely in the production of one body after another, it would never perform the task at hand. Now, it might be argued that an infinite regress is a fault only if this [being], being bodiless, were to begin creating its own body at the very moment of performing the action; however, in this case, it always already possesses a body.

Indeed, the body existing at the time of its activity is produced by that which was conjoined with a previous body, and that [previous body] likewise by one conjoined with an even earlier body; thus, this infinite regress does not constitute a fault, because the continuum of bodies is beginningless, like the sequence of seed and sprout. As they say: "They call it a fault only when it destroys the root," and so forth. That too is impure, because in all cases the destruction and production of the body are brought about by the conjunction of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen moral force).

For as long as the karma for the duration of one's life has been previously acquired, the body remains for that length of time. Furthermore, whatever kind of [karma] was acquired in that state, it arises accordingly in the subsequent existence; thus, everything is logical in the case of those such as us. But in the case of Īśvara, that is not so, because he is other than that—like a liberated soul (*muktātman*). Whence could such a conception of him arise? If it is argued that the divine Will indeed exists here, and by its power the destruction and production of that [body] will occur, it is not so.

Because this [creator] too acts everywhere in this context solely in dependence upon the unseen (adṛṣṭa); otherwise, it would be unnecessary to postulate an unseen force for everything, since the experience of pleasure and pain by living beings occurs exactly according to how the will of the Post (sthāṇu) operates. Therefore, even a body for him is not tenable; so how can there be an establishment of a specific form of God through the force of its presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatā)?

If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of the general property of intelligence (*buddhimattva-sāmānya*), which is inferred, when there is no specific [instance]?"—then why must there necessarily be a resolution for this? If it is argued, "That which is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be justified," then let that which is justified by means of something itself untenable rather remain untenable. If it is objected, "It is contradictory for that which is established by a *pramāṇa* to be untenable," then, in order to avoid contradiction, let there simply be a repudiation of its establishment by a *pramāṇa*.

Furthermore, there is no arising of that which has not arisen. How then is this a refutation of the proof (*sādhana*)? This is not a refutation of the proof; rather, it is a refutation of the proponent’s application (*yoga*). For he applies a proof to a generality of "being preceded by an intelligent agent" residing in the earth and so forth—which, due to the exclusion of specific qualities such as being endowed with mere consciousness, being endowed with desire and effort for the permanent and impermanent, and being embodied or bodiless—is like a flower in the sky and thus unfit to be proven.

And such a specific distinction is not possible, by relying upon which the general property of being preceded by an intelligent agent could be established in the case of the earth and so forth. Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of the abolition of all inference; for other inferences have as their object a specific feature that is indeed possible. For it is not the case that a specific fire located on the slope of a mountain is impossible.

Therefore, just as a person who, having unsheathed a sword in the darkness, brandishes it toward space might be restrained, yet neither the sword nor space is at fault; so too is the case with the Lord regarding the property of being an effect. Furthermore, that which was stated during the discussion on establishing the nature of time—that those who are the agents of something are necessarily cognizant of its material cause and other such factors, just like potters and the like, and that the Lord is the agent of all effects—is also untenable.

For, are these pot-makers fully cognizant of all the materials, instruments, and so forth required for their task, or are they cognizant of only a few materials, instruments, and so forth? The first position is not tenable, because it is impossible to have complete knowledge of the instruments, since the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa)—the instrumental cause of all things that come into being—is unknown. Nor are they cognizant of the specific recipient and purpose, because there exist many possible recipients, such as Devadatta and others, and many possible purposes, such as holding honey, water, or other liquids.

Now, if the cognition of God regarding the materials and instruments were merely a cognition of those materials and instruments in their entirety, then—just as potters and others possess only a cognition of the materials and instruments [for their specific tasks]—by that very same example, God too would possess only a cognition of those instruments. And if He possessed only that much cognition, His omniscience would not be established; for in that case, He would be a knower of only a few things. Furthermore, even such limited cognition is not established for God, as He would then be like a madman or the like. For instance:
He grunts, he moans, he roars, he sings, he pants, he withers, he becomes calm, and he fears.
He is bald, he plays, he laughs, he is weary, he blinks, he is fat, he is intoxicated, he is a drunkard. || 410 ||

Furthermore, he has no cognition of the tongue, palate, and other organs from which speech arises, for we observe that they function in their respective places without any intention on his part. As for the argument that there is no rule stating that whatever is an effect must necessarily produce the notion of having been produced within itself, and so forth—that too is not well-founded.

In the case of artificial gems, pearls, and the like, as well as in the earth that fills a pit, the existence of a similarity of configuration with non-artificial gems, pearls, regions of the earth, and so forth—which does not produce the cognition of them being artificial—is sufficient to account for the non-arising of that cognition; moreover, a similarity of uncreated configuration is not possible even in the case of the earth or mountains.

For you do not accept that there is such a thing as an uncreated configuration (*akṛtaka-saṃsthāna*). As for what was further stated—"What is this specific quality of being an effect? Is it the conformity to the positive and negative concomitance of an intelligent agent, or the observation thereof? and so forth—in that regard, this very thing is the specific quality of being an effect: that which is said to be intrinsically connected (*svabhāva-pratibaddha*) with an intelligent agent, which indeed produces in one the cognition that "it has been made" even though one has not seen it being made. And this point has already been explained previously.

As for what was also stated—that there is unity of the creator of earth and so forth—that too is not sound. For there is no certainty regarding the restriction of the intelligent probandum to unity. Indeed, its establishment through unity would occur only upon the establishment of its eternity, omnipresence, and omniscience; and only then would it be a fit recipient for the designation "Īśvara. Furthermore, the establishment of eternity and the other qualities is not possible.

For it is conceivable that a collection of effects occurring across different places and times is produced by multiple agents exceeding [the number] one. This being the case, there can be neither omnipresence nor eternity [of a single agent]. Furthermore, if the status of multiple agents is established merely as knowing their own respective materials (*upādāna*) and so forth, where is their omniscience? Moreover, when many individuals with conflicting intentions act together, the effect itself would simply not arise.

If it is argued that even if [the world] were produced, it would immediately perish, and thus this wretched triple world—whose activity at every moment consists merely in arising and perishing—could not perform any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), that is unconvincing. For such a suspicion might indeed apply to Īśvara and others, who are each endowed with qualities such as omnipotence; however, it is now asserted that not even one such being can be established.

Moreover, we observe that many agents with limited powers indeed initiate and complete a single or multiple effects. If you argue that—even in such cases—there must be one primary agent who is either more powerful or like a master builder or a general, and therefore agency belongs to him alone because the others merely follow his lead; we reply: no, for even there no such rule exists. We see that even independent beings, acting according to their own respective purposes, may come together to produce a single entity, such as a living being.

Even in that case, there is no such thing as a "first instigator," for even many individuals may have their hearts set on performing the same task without obstruction, or a lowly person might also become an instigator. Therefore, just as a single anthill or a mound of honey is produced by bees, honey-bees, ants, and other minute creatures, what need is there to mention the possibility of a single being creating the entire universe, including mountains like Maināka and Kailāśa? In this regard, mountains and the like, whose origins are not witnessed in this life, are sufficient proof of the existence of an intelligent agent; thus, the matter is settled by that alone.

And those living beings who are the agents of such things would proceed—just like anthill-dwelling insects—to act while perceiving the extremely minute substances of earth and so forth as the material cause (*upādāna*), the mouth and other parts as the instruments (*upakaraṇa*), the self itself as the recipient (*sampradāna*), and the maintenance and pleasure of the self as the purpose. Furthermore, since [the existence of] a controller is not established [as necessary], they would not necessarily be perceived, due to the remoteness of their nature. As for trees and the like whose birth is visible and which are of human origin, there is no need for further deliberation regarding them.

Furthermore, those regions surrounding the Vindhya mountains and elsewhere where human activity is not observed are also possessed of agents in the form of countless presiding spirits such as *piśācas* and the like; who, then, could be an omniscient knower? Moreover, since those presiding spirits are distinct according to place and time, how can they possess omnipresence and eternity? Nor is there any inference based on the force of reality (*vastubala*) that contradicts such a doubt.

But surely you yourselves have not accepted this either; and for those who conceive such an extremely difficult hypothesis, it would be better to simply postulate a Lord on account of parsimony (*lāghava*). [Reply: True. If the burden of proof were placed upon mere conceptualization, then we would indeed prioritize your own instruction. However, as long as you do not abandon the pretext of inference, we must necessarily apply ourselves to an exceedingly subtle investigation.

Now, if it pains the mind that the Narmadā and other rivers were created by countless minor beings, it would pain it even more that they were created by a single bodiless being. Therefore, valid cognition alone is everywhere more powerful; the status of an object remains exactly as valid cognition establishes it. For this reason, this is firmly established, and there is no concession whatsoever to minor beings.

Let the arrangement of the world be produced by hosts—whether minute or non-minute, invisible, of equal power or superior power, independent or subordinate, esteemed as primary, each accompanied by an individual creature, and consisting of infinite groups—who possess knowledge of only their own beginningless portion, who perform their respective tasks whether gross or subtle, single or manifold, and who are included within the four states of existence; let there not be a single creator for this. Nor should it be argued that a single creator is established because of the nature of being an effect, since the Jainas do not accept such a thing.

Because it would follow that even a single [instance] would not be established. Furthermore, in an inference that functions by the force of real entities (*vastubala*), there is no dependence upon the admission of another. Thus, when merely "one possessing intelligence" (*buddhimat*) is the probandum, the proof of the desired omniscient being—characterized by the necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyakatā*) with the knowledge of the material cause and so forth—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is because the necessity that all causal activity has a single substratum is unestablished.

Vācaspati, having established that a certain agent possesses knowledge of the body, the world, and so forth through the inference from the fact of being an effect, now sets forth a *pariśeṣa* (residual) inference—which is synonymous with *vyatireka* (negative concomitance)—for the purpose of proving his omniscience: "The agent who is the knower of the material causes and other factors of the body, the world, and so forth, cannot be one whose cognition is non-eternal and not all-encompassing; for if he were such, it would follow that he is ignorant of those very material causes and other factors. Indeed, no one like us is observed to be a knower of those material causes and so forth, yet this [agent] is a knower of those material causes and so forth."

Therefore, [the argument] "thus it is" should be understood as refuted by the logic already stated; for in this way, there is no certainty regarding its unity. Moreover, even if [the Lord] possesses impermanent and non-omniscient cognitions, it has been demonstrated that the perception of the material cause and so forth is possible [for him]. Now, one might object: since even a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is an effect, its creator must be one who is capable of perceiving the atoms that serve as its material cause. And those with the eye of flesh (*māṃsacakṣus*) cannot possibly be such [beings]. Otherwise, what wrong have we and others committed, that we do not become such?

Therefore, if one must necessarily accept that the creator of that [world] is a perceiver of supersensible objects, it is not logical to assume anyone other than Īśvara. This too is not tenable; for even though they possess eyes of flesh, the capacity of the sense organs is not common to all. For even among those far inferior to us, such as ants, vultures, wild boars, and others, an excellence in the acuity of the senses is observed. Indeed, some of the very smallest creatures may even possess the vision of atoms due to a particular power of their karma.

Just as ants perceive odors that are beyond our own range, it is not the case that anyone could perceive atoms—the subtlest of entities—nor could they see things remote in space or time, nor other subtle things, nor anything gross at all; for this has already been answered by the very example of the ants and so forth. If it is then argued: "Granted, there may be the possibility of perceiving an atom, but how could there be the perception of all the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) and the specific latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*) inherent in them?"

We say that this is not possible in any way. For the performance of an action is not invariably concomitant even with the thorough knowledge of the nature of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), as is seen in the case of a potter. Rather, the drawing forth [of the material] is desired by means of knowing the recipient (*sampradāna*) and the instruments (*upakaraṇa*). And that is impossible in the present case, because, according to the sequence already stated, the mere knowledge of those [elements] would suffice for the purpose. Furthermore, since he is being impelled by his own *karman*, it is unavoidable that he stands as the recipient (*sampradāna*), just as one says, "I am building a house for myself."
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of a logical deviation (vyabhicāra) by this very [example], because in that case activity occurs even without the cognition of another's intention to give.

[Objection: "Because of some reason, [the Lord] is the creator of his own temple; furthermore, even in the case of temples and the like, Paśupati alone is the agent, not someone like us. For Dhūrjaṭi is intent upon fashioning the entire aggregate of effects. He alone brings about everything, including dreams and so forth. Moreover, he is a knower of the intentions of others. [Response: This is incorrect. For, by such reasoning, it would follow that even potters and the like would not be agents, resulting in the absence of any illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) and the consequent impossibility of the inference from effect (kāryānumāna). Therefore, if agency must necessarily depend upon being the recipient of a gift (sampradānatā), [then the argument fails].

In that case, one’s own self must also be intended as the recipient (*sampradāna*). Or, let it be that another person alone is the recipient; nevertheless, the potter and others are not capable of knowing the true nature of that recipient—the *kṣetrajña*—apart from its manifestation in the form of a body characterized by such specific activities, which is what is conventionally established as the recipient. Nor can they know the various latent dispositions (*karmāśaya*) comprised under the term "instruments" (*upakaraṇa*).

In that case, just as a potter, knowing those various distinctions and being skilled in his implements through the very experience of the staff, wheel, and so forth, likewise even small creatures, though they are merely inferred [to exist], would become knowers of their own implements through the knowledge of pots and such; from where, then, could this [knowledge] come—the thorough cognition of the nature of the *kṣetrajña*, its merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and the distinctions of its latent dispositions (*āśaya*)? If it is asked: "How can there be a lack of connection with pots and such for a creator of earth and so forth who is bodiless?"

Since there is no possibility of a connection with supernatural powers (*siddhi*) for one who is bodiless, how can there even be a consideration of a connection with constituent parts (*aṅga*)? For if unity were established, the embodied being would be localized and incapable of all actions; thus, by implication, there might be hope for the establishment of a bodiless agent. However, it has already been stated that unity is difficult to prove. Or, let this [agent] be bodiless; even so, there is no fault.

[Objection: "But surely, since in the state of bodilessness instruments such as the staff, the wheel, the hand, or the mouth are impossible, it follows by the inference of elimination (*pāriśeṣyānumāna*) that the knowledge of those instruments must consist solely in the knowledge of the various latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*). [Reply: That is not well-said. For even space, time, inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth—which are included under the term 'instrument'—are known; and by the mere knowledge of these, the status of being an omniscient knower (*tajjñatāmātra*) is fulfilled. What, then, is this distinction, such that one who is not yet bodiless possesses the status of a knower of instruments through the knowledge of space and so forth alone, and not through the knowledge of *dharma* and the like?

If it is argued that [the agent] must know both [the instrument and its application], that is incorrect. For it is not observed that an agent must necessarily know every single instrument; nor do we maintain that the application of an instrument is established only through the knowledge of the directions and so forth, such that a specific inquiry into particulars would have to be made.

Rather, it is said that since the status of being an instrument can apply to the directions and so forth as well, and since the state of knowing the instruments is fulfilled by the mere knowledge of those [directions] alone, there is no need for the argument of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) to rest upon [the agent’s knowledge of the directions].

Therefore, just as in the case of successive makers [of objects like] a staff, a wheel, and so forth, where there is a succession of tools such as a shuttle and a loom, the status of being a knower of those tools is observed to exist through various external tools such as merit (*dharma*) and the like; so too, what should be the case here? Is it that [the status exists] by taking merit and the rest, or is there simply doubt? If, however, there were no other tool, then an explanation based on the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) would be appropriate.

Therefore, even if he were bodiless, there would be no non-perception of dharma and so forth through cognition; how much less so when that [bodiless state] itself is unestablished! Now, let it be granted that he lacks knowledge of dharma and so forth by virtue of possessing instruments; however, he will possess it necessarily by virtue of being a knower of effects. For the creator is the knower of that which is of the nature of an effect, and he alone is the Lord (*īśvara*). This too is not sound. For the "nature" (*rūpa*) of the effect is stated either as its mere essential form (*svarūpamātra*) or as qualified by its being the cause of dharma and adharma. It cannot be the first alternative.

For people performing acts such as giving or violence certainly experience [the results] merely by way of their own nature; yet they are not the lords [of those results]. Nor is the second case [tenable], because the determination of a thing's form as an effect does not necessarily follow for its maker simply by virtue of that thing being the cause of merit or demeror, as in the case of a potter. Indeed, a potter does not determine, "This pot is a cause of merit" or "This is a cause of demerit. Suppose, then, that in some particular effect there is a determination of it being a cause of merit or demerit.

If it is argued that there is the cognition that "this action such as giving is the cause of merit (*dharma*), whereas [action] such as violence is the cause of demerit (*adharma*)," this is indeed true in some cases. However, from this, an absolute proof [of the existence of a creator] does not follow; for we observe certain people performing actions even without such certainty. Since the performance of action is likewise possible here [in the case of the world], no one can possibly have knowledge of merit and demerit. And in the absence of such knowledge, how could there be a presiding controller over them?

Therefore, just as merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) are capable of producing their effects even without being presided over by a conscious agent (*cetanā*), so too will atoms and the like be capable of initiating the body and other effects; thus, there is no need for a conscious presider. If it is asked: "But how can insentient things such as atoms proceed of their own accord without being presided over by a conscious agent?"

Let it be granted for now that even though *dharma* and *adharma* are insentient, how can they act spontaneously without being presided over by a sentient being? This is the logic of the counter-objection (*pratibandinyāya*). But then, how does the Lord himself act? If you say, "He is sentient, therefore he acts with prior intelligence," then, acting for the sake of acquiring the desired and avoiding the undesired, he would not be the Lord because his purpose would remain unfulfilled.

Intentional activity necessarily entails both the desire to abandon what is to be avoided and the desire to acquire what is to be adopted. Wherever these two exist, there is the state of not having achieved one's purpose; and wherever there is the state of not having achieved one's purpose, there follows the lack of sovereignty.

Now, it might be argued that this undesirable consequence would indeed follow if activity were preceded by intelligence consisting of the desire to abandon what is to be discarded and the desire to acquire what is to be accepted; for [one might claim] that activity could occur through the desire to favor others. If that is so, then one who acts for the sake of others would always produce only happiness for all living beings, and never suffering. If it is argued that he produces both happiness and suffering because his agency is assisted by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), [we reply:]...

In that case, this [activity] does not proceed out of a desire to benefit others, but rather by the force of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). For it is accepted that whenever and wherever a desired or undesired auxiliary cause is present, [the agent] produces that [result] at that time and in that place. Indeed, if activity were driven by a desire to benefit others, then even when a cause of suffering is present, one would eliminate it and produce only happiness.

Now, liberation would occur through the exhaustion of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) by means of experiencing their fruits of pleasure and pain; therefore, [the Lord] produces both pleasure and pain. For His activity is solely for the sake of benefiting others, with the thought, "I shall liberate living beings from saṃsāra. And the liberation of the multitude of living beings results from the exhaustion of merit and demerit.

If it is argued that since the exhaustion of those [karmas] is not possible without the experience of their own fruits, the Supreme Lord—who is an ocean of boundless compassion—proceeds to create such bodies for torment and so forth; well then, are merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) also to be brought about by the operation of the Lord, or not? In the first case, having produced merit and demerit, it would have been better not to produce them at all than to subsequently cause their exhaustion.

Having produced these [beings] and then destroying them again, God does not differ from a commoner, following the logic of discarding a sweetmeat after washing away its impurities. Or how could he—knowing even what is evident to ordinary people that "it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off"—be omniscient? Furthermore, if God has no activity in the production of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), he would likewise have no activity in their destruction.

Just as with merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), pleasure and pain also arise from other causes without the operation of a Lord (*īśvara*), because merit and demerit can be exhausted through the experience of their results. Indeed, for the Lord as well, there is no agency in the exhaustion of merit and demerit other than the production of the results of pleasure and pain. Furthermore, if merit and demerit were not the effects of the Lord, then every reason adduced to establish the existence of the Lord would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, if the Lord acts for the sake of bringing about the liberation of living beings, how could he be the agent of the accumulation of unprecedented karma? This is not at all the case. Therefore, the activity of the Lord is not preceded by a deliberate intention.

If it is argued that this [insentient matter] proceeds precisely because it is its very nature, then, since consciousness—even though it exists—is a factor for activity, why is it not accepted that the nature belongs to the insentient alone? What is the point of postulating an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)? Consciousness, characterized by the thorough knowledge of the capacities of the causal factors, certainly possesses the status of being a factor with respect to activity; for in the absence of that thorough knowledge, the operation of a presiding agent would be impossible.

If it is argued that it is said to act "by its own nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*) because there is an absence of the volition [thinking], "I am doing this solely for my own sake or for the sake of another," then we ask: is the thorough knowledge of that agent's capacity concerned with the capacities of only a few factors (*kāraka*), or is it concerned with the capacities of all factors? In the first case, the presiding deity would not be omniscient. Furthermore, is this [knowledge] eternal or non-eternal?

If [the cognition] were eternal, then because the cognition of the causal capacity would be eternal, its effect would arise at all times. Now, if you argue that the effect arises not simply from the cognition of the causal capacity, but rather only when the cause is presided over by that [cognition], and that there is no rule stating that whatever is a cognition must necessarily be presided over [by another], but rather that it is the cognition itself that is presided over—then there is no fault. That is incorrect.

For "presiding" (adhiṣṭhitatva) is said to be the state of having come within the scope of effort. And since effort is also eternal, the production of its effect would occur at all times in that same state. Now, if that [effort] is non-eternal, then indeed, when a particular causal agent produces a particular effect, the cognition of its capacity also arises at that very time. That too is incorrect.

For if the causal factor itself practices the boldness of producing the effect, then what indeed remains to be done by the knowledge of its power, which would merely be present as something already established? Or, if it is said that the causal factor performs the effect at the time when a cognition arises whose object is the power of that causal factor—well then, what is the regulator for this cognition’s having as its object the specific power of a particular causal factor? Indeed, this [cognition] is neither sensory nor mental.

For it is logical that cognition arises wherever the sense organ or the mind extends; however, since the Lord lacks both sense organs and a mind, how can there be such a restriction? Suppose, then, that his knowledge has as its object the capacities of all causal factors (*kāraka*). Well then, is that [knowledge] also eternal or non-eternal? If it is non-eternal, [449]...

In that case, all effects would arise everywhere simultaneously, because the cognition of those [causes] is sequential. If [the cause] were eternal, then all effects would arise at all times and in all places. If it is argued that this is not so because of the absence of auxiliary factors (sahakārin) at all times and in all places, then the cognition of that [cause] does not function with respect to the capacities of all the causal factors.

But if activity depends on all auxiliary causes, whose own production is dependent upon that cognition [of the agent], why does it not arise at all times and in all places? If the production of the auxiliaries were likewise dependent upon that cognition, then the effect would also be so. If you argue that even though that cognition is non-sequential, its very nature is such that it produces something, somewhere, at some time, then the cognition does not serve as a factor for the activity.

Because the manifestation [of the effect] does not conform to that sequence [of the cause]. For whatever is the cause of something must conform to its sequence or non-sequence. Otherwise, if the effect were to arise sequentially even when the cause is non-sequential, or if the effect were to arise non-sequentially even when the cause is sequential, then by virtue of such independence, it would not be the effect of that cause at all.

Therefore, even though the thorough knowledge of that [object] is non-sequential, the activity arising sequentially makes its own nature alone the cause and appropriates it for itself, rather than the consciousness characterized by the thorough knowledge of that object. Thus, let there be activity even for the insentient by its very nature; enough with the postulation of a controller. If it is objected: "If an insentient thing acts without a controller, why would things such as a body not also act without being controlled? We reply: No.

If it were to proceed even without being supervised, why would laborers, servants, and the like not likewise proceed in that same way? If you argue that what is unsupervised does not proceed, then let it be the same for the body and so forth. If you ask, "Why would seeds and the like not likewise fail to proceed when unsupervised, just as the body and so forth do?"—then for you as well, why does the consequence not follow that the potter, the Lord, and others would also fail to act when unsupervised, just like the laborers and so forth?

Since we observe the activity of potters and the like even when they are not presiding over their tools, it follows that activity does not belong to that which is presided over. In that case, has activity ever been observed elsewhere to occur by virtue of a presider, such that the non-activity of seeds and the like when not presided over could be established? If it is argued that, although not perceived through direct perception, the activity of seeds and so forth when presided over is inferred—on the grounds of their insentience—by analogy with axes and other such tools; [we reply:]...

Likewise, why is it not accepted that even the activity of the potter, the lord, and so forth—which, though not perceptible, proceeds by virtue of a supervisor—is inferred through the reason of "sentience" based on their similarity to laborers, servants, and the like? For there is no distinction between the reasons of "sentience" and "insentience. If it is argued that there is indeed a distinction because the subject (pakṣa) is contradicted by perception, and thus the reason called "sentience" is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed/annulled by perception), [then we reply:

This is not so, because the fallacy of "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) applies equally even when proving insentience; for in the case of seeds and the like, the existence of a controller is contradicted by perception. If it is argued that there is no contradiction by perception regarding seeds and the like because the controller is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), then that is the same elsewhere as well, since the controllers such as potters and God are also beyond the senses. If it is argued that the experience "I act without being impelled" serves as a sublation (*bādhaka*) of the controller in the case of potters and the like—

It is not the case that [the existence of a supervisor] is impossible for one who is unknown, because even for an unseen mover, the status of being a mover is possible. Otherwise, how could there be the activity of animals and the like, who do not know the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as their mover? Therefore, since you wish to establish the existence of a supervisor—even though it is imperceptible—in seeds and so forth by means of the reason "consciousness," you must accept the establishment of the existence of a supervisor for the entire class of conscious beings, including those distinct from laborers and the like, because there is no difference [in the application of the reason].

Furthermore, by postulating the existence of one supervisor after another in this manner, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and thus no production of effects would occur even over many thousands of aeons. Now, it might be argued that since an insentient entity cannot act on its own with spatial and temporal regularity, it is logical to establish the existence of a supervisor for seeds and the like based on the reason of their being insentient; however, this is not the case for the potter or the Lord (*īśvara*) based on the reason of their being sentient.

If it is argued that [the body] exists because its activity occurs according to the constraints of place and time even in the absence of a conscious controller, that is incorrect. For it has already been established that the restriction of activity occurs for an insentient thing even without a controller; furthermore, being insentient does not function as a necessary condition for the existence of a controller. Therefore, since the coexistence of being controlled and being insentient is observed in certain insentient things such as threads and the like, you must admit that being insentient serves as a probans [for the existence of a controller].

If it is argued that there is no observation of coexistence anywhere between "being insentient" and "being presided over by a conscious agent," then the latter must be accepted as a probans for the former; otherwise, it should not be accepted in this case either. For it is more reasonable to hold that the conscious agent exists only where its presiding is observed, and not elsewhere. By this, the following arguments are also refuted: that which was stated beginning with "by obtaining occasional and various auxiliary causes," and so forth; and that beginning with "merit and demerit function being presided over by a conscious agent because they are insentient," and so forth.

Furthermore, would the insentience (*acetanatva*) of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) be absolute or relative? In the first case, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished for the opponent; for the Jains accept that merit and demerit are in some way sentient, being non-different in some respect from the conscious self (*ātman*). In the second case, however, it is unestablished for the proponent; for you do not establish that merit and demerit are in any way insentient.
[451] Furthermore, regarding the convention (*samaya*) which was stated as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the establishment of the moon’s crescent:
Now, my friend, would you say that its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is extrinsic (parataḥ) or intrinsic (svataḥ)? || 411 ||

The determination of its validity may arise from correspondence with a prior conceptual construction, from the absence of contradiction, or from the fact that it was spoken by a reliable person. (412)
There is no consensus here [regarding supersensible matters] because all the stated proofs have failed;

yet, there is such consensus in some single instance within the realm of the perceptible. If that is so, what of it? For even among the Lokāyatas, it is not the case that not a single truth has been uttered.
Furthermore, in that treatise, it is because he would be true from every side.

Furthermore, how could the absence of non-conformity (visaṃvāda) here reach the status of a definitive conclusion? If you should say that it is so in some cases due to the lack of observation [of contrary instances], then because of its being a system (tantra), that [absence of non-conformity] would deviate with respect to the universe as a whole.
Without those who know all things, no one else is able to understand [this]. || 414 ||
But if the certainty of its validity is based on it being spoken by a trustworthy person, then how could liberation occur? For this would incur the fault known as mutual dependence. (415)

For when the existence of a trustworthy person is established, the word spoken by him would possess the status of valid cognition; and when that [validity] exists, the establishment of the trustworthy person would be free from blemish. (416)
The followers of Akṣapāda did not accept that convention has the status of a valid means of knowledge *in itself*.
How, then, could the proof of Purāri [Śiva] from scripture be acceptable to the wise? (417)
And thus,

this very bow-staff of manifold arguments such as "being an effect" and so forth, which was clearly [standing firm], has now been shattered in an instant, pierced by the woodworms of flawed refutations.
Therefore, how could he whose singular intellect is intent on the creation of all worlds be one who knows only women? Without a doubt, it is by his power that [the world exists]. 418.
Some float right outwards, while others reach the middle.
And even the water from the jar-born [Agastya] might exist for one who would rashly drink this ocean of debate.
[452] Here, a certain follower of Kapila says: "Even today, the system of the Kāpilas maintains its established position."
How can those who proclaim [him] as the Lord establish him as the Lord? || 420 ||

And thus Patañjali says: "The Lord (Īśvara) is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions (kleśa), actions (karman), their fruitions (vipāka), and latent dispositions (āśaya). Among these, ignorance (avidyā), egoism (asmitā), attachment (rāga), aversion (dveṣa), and the will to live (abhiniveśa) are the afflictions. Ignorance is the perception of the eternal, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self. Egoism is the very identity of the power of the seer (dṛk-śakti) and the power of seeing (darśana-śakti). The power of the seer is the Self (ātman), and the power of seeing is the intellect (buddhi); that which is the identity of these two through delusion is egoism. Attachment is that which clings to pleasure.

Non-attachment (*aparāga*) is a mental factor characterized by an adherence to pleasure. Hatred (*dveṣa*) is that which lies latent within suffering; it is well known as hatred when there is an insistence on the desirability of abandoning an object that produces suffering. Clinging (*abhiniveśa*) is a natural flow that is firmly rooted even in the wise. "Natural flow" means independent of external causes; this clinging is firmly rooted in that very manner not only for the ignorant but for the wise as well—just as living beings, from birth onwards, possess a fear of death. Actions (*karman*) are those that are wholesome and unwholesome.
