Its maturation consists of birth, lifespan, and experience. The latent dispositions (*āśaya*) are the various types of formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) that correspond to those [maturations]. He who is untouched—that is, not defiled—by these is the Lord (*īśvara*). Nor should it be argued that, because the state of being untouched by these is common to them, the status of being the Lord would follow for liberated souls (*muktātman*); for it is impossible for them to ever be untouched by bondage, since the threefold bondage—known as *prākṛtika*, *vaikārika*, and *dākṣiṇa*—exists prior to their liberation.

In that regard, for those who worship *prakṛti* out of ignorance regarding the Self within *prakṛti*, there is bondage consisting of *prakṛti*. For it is said concerning those merged in *prakṛti* in the *Purāṇa*: "Those who contemplate the Unmanifest remain for a full hundred thousand [years]. The *vaikārika* (evolutive) bondage belongs to those who, through the intellect of a person (*puruṣa*), worship only the evolutes—the elements, the senses, the ego, and the intellect. Concerning them, this is said: "Those who contemplate the senses remain here for ten intermediate periods (*manvantaras*)."

"But those devoted to material things remain for a full hundred years; those possessed of self-conceit, for a thousand; and those devoted to the Buddha remain for a hundred thousand years, free from the fever of suffering. Thus, regarding the merit of sacrifices and public works (*iṣṭāpūrta*), the teacher of the Southern school says: "One who performs sacrifices and public works, though knowing the principles of the person (*puruṣatattva*), is bound because his mind is struck by desire.

By means of these three bonds, the Blessed Lord remains forever untouched by them, like the moon, which is never stained by its own digits. Others, however, having uprooted these three bonds of their own by means of discriminative knowledge, are liberated. For the eternally liberated Lord, there is no prior limit of bondage, as there is for the souls of transmigrating beings who have been released; nor is there a subsequent limit, as there is for yogis who have merged into primordial nature (*prakṛti*) despite possessing knowledge of reality.

For even after attaining liberation, they are born again as subjects of bondage. Or, this one is the Lord (*īśvara*) by virtue of possessing sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). That sovereignty is of eight kinds. Namely: *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, *mahimā*, *prāpti*, *prākāmya*, *vaśitva*, *īśitva*, and *yatra-kāmāvasāyitva*. Among these, *aṇimā* is the state of being minute; because of it, being invisible to all beings, he moves everywhere in the world. *Laghimā* is the state of being light.

Because, by taking hold of the rays of the sun, one goes to the world of the sun; its greatness becomes vast, since even that which is small is connected with the dimensions of the serpent-world, the mountains, the cities, and the sky. Because of attainment (*prāpti*), all things become present; for example, while standing on the very ground, one touches the moon with the tip of a finger. Irresistible will (*prākāmya*) is the non-obstruction of one's desire; because of it, one sinks into and emerges from the earth as if in water.

Mastery (*vaśitva*) is that by which one becomes a master, independent, with respect to the primary elements such as earth and their derivatives such as cows and jars. Lordship (*īśitva*) is that because of which one has power over the origination, maintenance, and destruction of both the primary elements and their derivatives. Wherein lies the power to resolve at will (*yatra-kāmāvasāyitva*), since there is the state of having true resolve; for in whatever manner his resolve is directed toward the elements, in that very manner the elements become.

For while in other cases determinations conform to the objects to be determined, here it is that the objects to be determined conform to His determination. Furthermore, His activity is for the sake of destroying and favoring all transmigrating beings; for He, possessing supreme wisdom, remains resolved: "I shall rescue the entire world during the kalpa-dissolutions and the great universal dissolutions. And when He is recited by yogins with the expressive syllable *praṇava*, He bestows upon them their desired fruit.

And because he is not limited by time, He is the teacher even of the ancient great sages such as Kapila; for they are indeed delimited by time—such as the Kalpa, Mahākalpa, and so forth—but the Lord is not. He alone, whose single nature is eternal, perfectly governs this entire triple world of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ at every moment.
Therefore, that Lord Kapālin is perfected; endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers such as atomization and levitation, he is indeed not touched by karma or afflictions here. [421]
What has been spoken by you here, whose mind is skilled in the fabrication of dream-activities and who is dull-witted through faith— [that is what follows].
O friend, you whose intellect is bound to the Kapila system, listen now with attention as that [system] is being refuted. (422)

For that which was asserted by her, beginning with "by the afflictions" (*kleśa*) and so forth, does not enter the path of logical reasoning. This is because his essential nature (*svarūpa*) consists merely in being untouched by the afflictions and so forth, or else it consists in omniscience (*aśeṣajñatva*) while that [untouched state] exists. In the first case, he would be nothing other than a liberated soul (*mukta*), because he is untouched by them, just like any other liberated soul; he would not, however, be the Lord (*īśvara*). Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even those other liberated souls would be Lords.

In that case, since he is eternally untouched [by objects], his essential nature must be stated as omniscience. How is that established? Is it from being the creator of all things, or from being the locus of sovereignty? Regarding the first position: does he perform every effect independently, or is he dependent upon *prakṛti*? That too is not well-argued; for *prakṛti* is unestablished by its very nature, and its non-establishment will be refuted hereafter.

Furthermore, the dependence of the Three-Eyed One (Śiva) upon primordial matter (*prakṛti*) would have to be due either to the imparting of excellence [to him] by matter or to their acting together toward a single effect. The first position is not tenable; for it is impossible to impart excellence to Śaṅkara, who is entirely eternal and immutable. The second position is also not superior; because it would entail the simultaneous production of all effects.

Because the pair of causes—Śaṅkara and Pradhāna—possess unimpeded power and are eternally present, they constitute a complete causal complex for those [effects]. Now, even though this pair of causes is eternally present, all effects do not arise simultaneously; for the three qualities (guṇas) residing in Pradhāna, beginning with rajas, serve as the auxiliary conditions for Īśvara. And since these [qualities] manifest their activity successively, there is also a succession among the effects.

For instance, when *bhargas* (the luminous principle) is joined with *rajas* whose activity has become manifest, it is then the cause of the creation of effects; when it is conjoined with *sattva* of that same kind, it is then the cause of their maintenance; and when this [principle] is again united with *tamas* of such a nature, it is then the cause of their dissolution—if this is your argument, [455]...

That too is incorrect. For, do Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) possess the power to produce any one among creation, maintenance, or dissolution, or not? If they do, then even at the time of creation, there would follow the occurrence of maintenance and dissolution, because their causes are complete, just as in the case of creation. Likewise, at the time of maintenance, there would follow creation and dissolution; and at the time of dissolution, there would follow creation and maintenance. And this is not tenable, because it contradicts empirical experience.

Now, if there is no capacity [for activity], then only one among the effects such as creation and so forth would exist eternally; for those two possess the capacity to produce that specific effect, but not others, because it is impossible for them to have the capacity to produce anything else. Furthermore, since these two are unchanging, the arising of a new capacity in them is a contradiction; otherwise, their nature as eternal and unitary would be undermined. Moreover, the manifestation of the functions of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas* must be either eternal or non-eternal. It cannot be eternal, because it occurs only occasionally.

Furthermore, because it would entail the consequence that creation and so forth occur simultaneously. If, on the other hand, it is impermanent, from what would it arise? From *prakṛti* and the Lord (*īśvara*) alone, or from something else, or independently? In the first case, there is the undesirable consequence that it would exist at all times, because the cause called *prakṛti* and the Lord is eternally present due to its permanence. If it arises from something else, that too would contradict your own tenets, since you do not admit any cause other than *prakṛti* and the Lord.

In the third alternative, however, there is a contradiction regarding its manifestation due to the restriction of place and time; for it is impossible for that restriction to apply to something that exists independently. Indeed, only those entities whose activity depends on other factors can be occasional, because their existence and non-existence are tied to the presence and absence of those [factors]. Others are not so, because they lack anything upon which they must depend. Alternatively, if there were something to be depended upon, there would be a contradiction to its arising independently.

Therefore, even if he were dependent on primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the Three-Eyed One would not be the performer of all effects. Or, if his agency is admitted, then the definition of the Self—namely, that "he is non-agent, devoid of qualities, and pure"—would be untenable. If it is argued that this definition belongs only to other selves and not to the Lord, because He is distinct from them, and thus there is no such fault; [we reply: in that case, since purity and so forth would not constitute His essential nature, His distinction from them would be extreme indeed.

Therefore, since the status of being the creator of all things cannot be established in any way whatsoever when examined in the case of the Three-eyed One (Śiva), his omniscience is not proven on that basis. Nor is it proven because he is the locus of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). For sovereignty in that regard would have to be either innate or produced by primordial nature (*prakṛti*). It cannot be innate, because the Sāṃkhyas accept it as a property of the intellect (*buddhi*).

For they have accepted consciousness alone as the inherent nature of the self. Now, if [consciousness] were produced by *prakṛti*, then indeed, when *prakṛti* transforms into a modification characterized by the intellect (*buddhi*), specific states of the intellect such as virtue, knowledge, and power manifest. This too is not tenable, because in this way you yourself have demonstrated the absence of sovereignty in the Lord.

Indeed, if the sovereignty of the transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*) were impossible, it would not be logical for that [sovereignty] to belong to the Lord of Beings (*bhūtapati*), who is a distinct entity from it; for then it would follow that it belongs to any other self as well. If it is argued that it belongs to him alone and not to another because of his connection with the intellect, [we ask]: what is this connection between Time and the intellect on the part of the Lord? Is it inherence (*samavāya*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), or something else, such as mere activity directed toward the Lord? It cannot be inherence.

Because a property belonging to one thing cannot logically reside in another. Whatever is the property of a certain thing does not inhere in anything other than that; for example, consciousness is the property of the *puruṣa*. And since the intellect (*buddhi*) is a property of *prakṛti*, it cannot inhere in something other than that, even if such a thing were possible. Nor is there an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntika*) based on the redness and so forth inhering in a crystal and the like; for when a *japā* flower is in proximity, it is the crystal itself that undergoes transformation in that way.

This will be demonstrated in detail on the occasion of examining the arising of the [causal] connection (*pratibandha*). Furthermore, if it is admitted that the Self (*ātman*), having transformed into the form of the intellect (*buddhi*) through the proximity of *prakṛti*, undergoes such a transformation, there would be a contradiction with the accepted doctrine that [the Self] is "powerless," "unchanging" (*apariṇāmin*), and "non-transmigrating" (*apratisaṅkrama*). Therefore, a relationship characterized by inherence (*samavāya*) between the intellect and God is not tenable. Nor is it of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because the intellect is not a substance (*adravyatva*) and because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

A connection with the intellect certainly exists through all selves, which are eternal and all-pervading. By this, conjunction-inherence (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) and other such relations are also refuted, because the impossibility [of those] and the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) are no different here as well. If it is argued that its relation to him is merely the fact of its proceeding for the sake of the Lord (*īśvara*), that too is incorrect, because its proceeding for the sake of the Lord is impossible.

For the modifications such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth attain manifestation when primordial nature (*prakṛti*) proceeds by the force of the necessity of fulfilling the purposes of the person (*puruṣārtha*). However, there is no purpose of the person to be accomplished for the Lord (*īśvara*). And if this [nature] were not active, how could His lordship (*aiśvarya*) be possible? Therefore, His omniscience is established even from the fact that He is the substratum of lordship.
Thus, everything from "And because of His connection with lordship, He is the Lord" up to "Is He, then, the Lord? is to be understood as having been refuted.
O Sāṅkhya, thus has this entire series of prima facie arguments correctly set forth by you been refuted at such length.

And thus, these reports of the attainment of perfection by those who wear the crescent moon as their crest-jewel have suddenly vanished into the interior of your fame, even as we were looking on. (423) 26.
Having set aside all the doctrines of the non-Buddhists through reasoning, this proof for the existence of the Omniscient One has been formulated in this manner.
Therefore, it is entirely logical that his omniscience cannot possibly be established by means of his eating morsels of food again.
To him who was speaking thus, [the author] replied:
"Nor does his lack of omniscience follow from the fact that he consumes solid food (kavalāhāra), because there is no contradiction between consuming solid food and being omniscient. || 27 ||
[This refers] to that Arhat. The remainder [of the text] has its meaning clear.

Now, the claim "because there is no contradiction" is unestablished (*asiddha*), because there exists an inference (*anumāna*) that proves the contradiction between those two. To explain: the subject of dispute, the *kevalin*, does not possess solid food (*kavalāhāra*), because he is of a different class (*vijātīya*) from one who possesses cognitive obscuration (*chadmastha*). Furthermore, whoever possesses solid food is not of a different class from one who possesses cognitive obscuration, such as ourselves and others. And since the *kevalin* is of a different class from one who possesses cognitive obscuration, therefore he does not possess solid food. Nor should the unestablished nature of the reason (*hetu*) be raised here.

This is because the proponent and the opponent both accept that the omniscient one (kevalin) is of a different nature from one who is still under the veil of ignorance (chadmastha). Otherwise, it would follow that the omniscient one, like one under the veil of ignorance, would likewise not be omniscient. Nor should one suspect that the thesis is contradicted by the inference: "The omniscient one does not possess solid food (kavalāhāra), because he possesses a body, like us and others. This is because the reason—possessing a body—is inconclusive due to the case of the gods (*tridaśa*) and others; for they possess bodies, yet they do not consume solid food.

For they are established in the supreme scripture as possessing a type of sustenance distinct from morsel-food (*kavalāhāra*). Now, one might object: "If the state of possessing morsel-food is not admitted for the *kevalin*, then how could there be the designation of 'grossness' (*audārikatva*) regarding his body? This is not to be doubted. Indeed, the wise do not maintain that the designation of grossness in this case is based on the consumption of morsel-food; rather, it is based on the fact that [the body] is composed of primary matter (*pudgala*).

It is "gross" (*audārika*) because it is undertaken by the most prominent individuals among the entire mass of persons (*pudgala-rāśi*), according to its etymological derivation. Furthermore, they have asserted that the white-robed Kevalins (Śvetāmbaras) possess solid food (*kavalāhāra*), based on the scriptural statement: "All living beings, from those with one sense-organ up to those with subtle senses and those possessing *sa-yoga-kevala* [omniscience], are consumers of food. However, that too is merely a manifestation of their failure to understand the meaning of the scriptures.

For in that sūtra, because the Blessed One, though possessed of omniscience (*kevalin*), is mentioned alongside those with only one sense-faculty (*ekendriya*) and others, and because of the teaching on continuous nourishment, what is intended by "eating" (*āhāra*) is merely the taking up of matter (*pudgala*) suitable for the body. Otherwise, the Blessed One, as a possessor of omniscience, would have to subsist on solid food (*kavalāhāra*) continuously; and this is not even desired by you yourselves.

It is argued that even though the Sūtra provides an exposition alongside those with one sense-faculty (*ekendriya*) and others, and although it teaches uninterrupted nourishment, the existence of food is established according to what is possible; thus, for an omniscient one (*kevalin*), even the consumption of morsel-food (*kavalāhāra*) is established as occurring only occasionally. Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that his body could not persist for a long time, just as it does not for people like us. This [argument] is also unable to withstand scrutiny. For in this way, even the ascertainment of omniscience would be difficult to attain therein.

For in those such as ourselves, whose bodies are sustained by solid food (kavalikāhāra), only non-omniscience is observed. Furthermore, it is heard in the scriptures that there is a supreme endurance of the gross body even without solid food, as exemplified by the First Lord of the Tīrtha and others.
To illustrate: it is said that in former times, the illustrious Jina Śrī Nābheya rolled upon his broad shoulders...
Playfully bearing a mass of matted locks as dark as the waters of the Kālindī.
Immediately upon his renunciation, he remained without food for a full year, dwelling alone in various regions where Mlecchas predominated. [425]
Thus the venerable sage Bāhubali was surrounded by various kinds of birds, whose rows of nests were formed by the profusion of their quivering beards and fluttering feathers hanging down as pendants.

O friend, while established in the practice of *kāyotsarga* with a steady mind, how many ascetics did he perform year-long fasts of such extraordinary intensity? What more need we say of others like him? 426.

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a fixed limit for the duration of the maintenance of a gross body in the absence of solid food (*kavalikāhāra*). Consequently, since there is no basis for formulating alternative interpretations of the sūtras that teach the intake of food by one-sensed beings and others, let the meaning of the sūtras be understood exactly as they are heard. Moreover, when an omniscient being (*kevalin*) consumes solid food, does he do so out of hunger, or because the maintenance of the body would otherwise be impossible, or simply by his very nature? These three possibilities stand opposed to one another, their respective powers neutralized. [460] And there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a fixed limit for the duration of the maintenance of a gross body in the absence of solid food (*kavalikāhāra*). Consequently, since there is no basis for formulating alternative interpretations of the sūtras that teach the intake of food by one-sensed beings and others, let the meaning of the sūtras be understood exactly as they are heard. Moreover, when an omniscient being (*kevalin*) consumes solid food, does he do so out of hunger, or because the maintenance of the body would otherwise be impossible, or simply by his very nature? These three possibilities stand opposed to one another, their respective powers neutralized.
The various philosophical positions prevail by resorting to a similarity with the three eyes of the Three-Eyed One.

The first position is not tenable; for since hunger is of the nature of suffering, it cannot occur in a Kevalin when the entire collection of defects that cause suffering has been eliminated. Alternatively, if the defects were not eliminated, then the mass of suffering born of those defects would arise, and absolute bliss would be impossible there. No sensation equal to hunger can possibly exist in the body, because:
[461] "As long as there is talk of the multitude of virtues, so long does the curiosity for expansion persist..."
To the same extent that there is familiarity with love, to that same extent is there cultivation of modesty;
to that same extent are there compositions of speech, and to that same extent does the intellect expand. 428.

Now, the second position is that [the existence of the body] is otherwise inexplicable; however, this too is not tenable. For it is possible for the Blessed One, the Kevalin of infinite power, to maintain his physical body even without solid food (kāvalikāhāra). Furthermore:

those who are capable of fashioning the earth—even though it is crowded with great mountain ranges, forests, rivers, ramparts, and oceans—into something possessing the beautiful luster of a parasol...
O good friend, it is thus determined by the mind that they lack the power to remain in their own state without experiencing the Meru as a staff-like [support], even for the sake of enjoyment. (429)

Since there is no fault in the aforementioned enjoyment when it is conceived as having the nature already described, this "morsel-enjoyment" (kavalabhukti) rests upon the burden of contradiction with the Jina-elephant; therefore [it is rejected].
How is it that these [ascetics], whose bodies are marked with white garments, have here displayed their devotion in vain? (430)
A certain gaze, characterized by the skill of a directional-cloth wearer (dikpaṭa), was observed, greedy for the destruction of mouthfuls of food.
O friend, for a single moment, behold this [state] of ours which is somehow eager to rescue him. 431.

For instance: as for the proof presented—namely, "because of being of a different nature from one in a state of concealment (*chadmastha*)" and so forth—in order to establish the contradiction between physical food and omniscience—it is here questioned: is the Kevalin (the possessor of absolute knowledge) admitted by you to be entirely of a different nature from one in a state of concealment, or only in some respect? In the first alternative, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) in its own nature for both the proponent and the opponent.

This is because both parties agree that the Blessed One shares a commonality with one who is still in the state of a *chadmastha* (an obscured being) through such properties as being a living being (*trasatva*), possessing five senses (*pañcendriyatva*), being non-human (*anuṣyatva*), and being male (*puruṣatva*). Furthermore, in the second alternative, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because even in the case of the opposite side—such as ourselves, who possess physical food intake (*kavalāhāra*)—there exists some degree of dissimilarity (*vijātīyatva*) from one who is still in the state of a *chadmastha*.

Indeed, [the omniscient one] is not in every respect of the same class as an obscured person (*chadmastha*) such as ourselves, because that would contradict experience and result in the undesirable consequence of identity. If it is argued that the omniscient one is somehow of a different class from the obscured person by virtue of the property of being non-obscured (*achadmasthatva*), and therefore there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*)—since the reason "being of a different class" does not apply to us and others insofar as we are obscured—then that is quite untenable, for it falls under the stain of being "inconclusive due to doubt" (*sandigdhānaikāntikatva*).

The contradiction with the subject under discussion (the reason) is not established in relation to physical food (kavalāhāra). Indeed, the presence and absence of physical food are not caused by being in a state of non-omniscience (chadmasthatva) or being in a state of omniscience (achadmasthatva); rather, they are caused by the presence and absence of the faculties such as the sense of taste, the gross body, and the completion (paryāpti) of the experience of the taijasa-karma and so forth. This will be demonstrated, as it is observed to be so among people like us and among perfected beings (siddhas).

As for the inference that was raised and refuted—namely, that "the Kevalin possesses solid food (kavalāhāra) because he is embodied, like us and others"—that is merely a criticism of something not accepted [by the opponent]. For we do not accept that mere embodiment is the cause of possessing solid food in the Kevalin; rather, it is a specific collection of conditions such as the *paryāpti*s (developmental capacities). Since that [collection] has not yet ceased in him, how could the absence of solid food be possible there?

As for what was stated—that indeed, in that case, [the designation "gross"] is not based on the consumption of morsel food (*kavalāhāra*), and so forth—even if the designation "gross" applied to the body of the Blessed One is based on its being composed of a preeminent person (*pradhānapudgala*), this does not establish the absence of the aforementioned eating in the Blessed One, because it is impossible to exclude that [eating] which is based on its own causes. Furthermore, as for what was said—that [the Blessed One lacks such eating] because of his mention alongside those with [only] five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) and because of the teaching of uninterrupted eating.

This too is merely a manifestation of the non-trivial obsession with envy on the part of the Āśāmbaras. For just as, even though our own kind and others are mentioned alongside those with a single sense-organ (*ekendriya*) and so forth, and even though there is instruction regarding uninterrupted food, the *kavalāhāra* (mouthful-eating) is not contradicted; likewise, it is not contradictory for a *kevalin* [to have such food]. Nor should it be said that there is no consideration of food at all for our own kind and others in this sūtra; for they are indicated by the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*) in the phrase "beginning with those with one sense-organ. Therefore, what is intended here is food in its general sense.

In that regard, if even morsel-food (kavalāhāra) were to be present in a Kevalin due to its own causes, then what indeed would be impaired? Even the scripture which is heard—such as "The Kevalins who have attained omniscience enter the state of vigrahagati"—is entirely consistent with the Kevalin’s consumption of morsel-food.

In this context, it is stated that beings other than those undergoing the process of physical embodiment (vigrahagati) and so forth are "nutriments" (*āhāraka*) by virtue of mere nutriment (*āhāramātra*). In that case, there is no contradiction even with respect to morsel-food (*kavalāhāra*); for if there were a contradiction, then for you as well, such a kind of nutriment would necessarily follow, resulting in the absurd consequence that every day, at every house, you would be confronted by the obstruction of consuming delicious, succulent food made smooth with abundant, dripping clarified butter, offered from the lotus-hands of those who are not faithful (*aśrāddha*), yet are charmingly connected to the faith of the awakened and the pure.

Now, if it is argued that even here [in this system], just as is possible, the *kavalāhāra* (solid food) is postulated for those like us based on the established nature of food, but not for the *kevalin* (the omniscient one); well then, from what cause is the impossibility of *kavalāhāra* for the *kevalin* derived? If it is argued that it is due to the absence of delusion (*moha*), we say no; for the status of hunger as a cause of delusion will be refuted later. Furthermore, as for what was said—that otherwise the Blessed One, the *kevalin*, would have to be continuously consuming solid food—that too is not well-established.

Because a distinguished food arises from a distinguished cause, and because such a distinguished cause is impossible at every moment, it is logical that the Blessed One’s consumption of solid food (*kavalāhāra*) occurs only occasionally. However, as for the food characterized by the intake of *pudgala* (nutritive essence), such as the nourishment through body hair and so forth, its presence there even at every moment is not contradictory, since its activity depends on its own causes which arise at every moment. Furthermore, whatever else was suspected—namely, that the arrangement of food is established according to possibility and so forth—is indeed logically consistent.

For indeed, until nearly ten million years [of age], the maintenance of a gross body is not possible without superior food. If it is argued that this [maintenance] is possible for the Kevalin because his lifespan is non-accidental (*nirupakrama*), then surely that state of having a non-accidental lifespan exists even during the stage of the *chadmastha* (the soul with veils); therefore, why would he take food even then? For the maintenance of the body is possible even without it.

Do you intend to suggest that being free from the onset of premature death (*nirupakramāyuṣkatva*) is not the cause for the persistence of the body? It is not so. Rather, our intention is this: just as he experiences [pleasure] during the state of being a non-omniscient (*chadmastha*) due to the presence of its own causes—even though he is free from the onset of premature death—how can he be denied [the experience] while experiencing it in the state of omniscience (*kevali*) for that very same reason?

If it is argued that in the state of being a non-omniscient he performs the act of eating (*kavalana*) because of an excess of greed arising from the tasting of sweet and other flavors produced by the power of the deluding karma (*mohanīyakarma*), whereas in the state of omniscience this does not occur because of the absence of such [delusion]—[we reply: ...

[464] That is not tenable. For indeed, even during the state of being a *chadmastha* (one still under the veil of ignorance), it is not the *mohanīya* karma that produces the act of eating; rather, it is the *vedanīya* and other such karmas. Consequently, while there may be an absence of capacity for eating due to the non-existence of *mohanīya* in the state of a *kevalin*, how can the actual act of eating—which is brought about by its own specific causes—be denied even in that state? Furthermore, there is no absolute difference in the nature of the body between the state of a *chadmastha* and the state of a *kevalin*.

By this [power], even in the absence of ordinary food, the maintenance of that body would not be contradictory; for even the excellence of knowledge and so forth continues until the fall of that very body, which remains sustained by its prior bone-joints and other factors.

It is established everywhere by the means of valid cognition known as reasoning arising from perception and non-perception that the maintenance of a superior gross body—such as ours—is caused by superior food; therefore, if a superior gross body were to exist elsewhere even in the absence of superior food, then that [maintenance] would never be based on superior food, because an effect can never arise even once from what is not its cause.

If, moreover, the maintenance of a distinct gross body among beings such as ourselves—which is caused by specific food—were to occur in some particular person even in the absence of specific food, then smoke produced from fire in a kitchen or similar place might also occur on the slopes of a mountain or elsewhere without fire. Consequently, the inference of fire and so forth from smoke and so forth would be untenable due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Indeed, smoke of this kind is established as originating from fire of this kind by a single application of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operating everywhere, through the force of its being determined as an effect; for if it were to exist from something other than the nature of fire, it would not arise even once from fire, because it would be distinct from the nature of fire.

If it is argued that smoke arises from the very nature of fire in places such as a kitchen, and thus smoke is produced everywhere and always solely from the nature of fire—because that which is not produced from it does not have the nature of smoke, and therefore there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the inference of fire from smoke and the like—that is not so; for this same logic applies elsewhere as well. For if a specific maintenance of a gross body were to occur even without a specific kind of food, then that would not truly be a specific maintenance of a gross body.

Furthermore, it has already been stated that she (the smoke) is not absolutely of a different genus (*atyantavijātīyatva*) from the solitary [fire]. However, absolute homogeneity (*sarvathā samānajātīyatva*) is impossible even between the smoke perceived on a kitchen hearth and the smoke perceived on the neck of a mountain.

Therefore, just as in the case of people like us, even for a Kevalin, the maintenance of the gross body for an extended period of time is not possible without solid food (kāvalikāhāra). Consequently, whatever maintenance of a specific gross body exists cannot occur without a specific type of nourishment, just as is the case with people like us. Furthermore, the inference proceeds thus: "The Kevalin who is the subject of dispute possesses a specific maintenance of a gross body. Otherwise, even the inference of fire from smoke and so forth would not be possible.

That too is merely a manifestation of dogmatic insistence; for there is no possible contradiction between omniscience—which arises from the destruction of the destructive karmas (*ghātikarma*)—and the presence of solid food (*kavalāhāra*) or its effects, such as the maintenance of a gross physical body (*audārika-śarīra*) over a very long period, in one who possesses that omniscience. As for what was stated, beginning with "Furthermore, it is heard... and ending with "...there exists a proof establishing the fixed duration of the maintenance of the gross physical body," [that is also refuted].

That too is the prattle of one whose mind is agitated by swallowing the *kālakūṭa* poison of intense dogmatic attachment surging from the bottomless ocean of non-comprehension. For if the authority of the scripture (*samaya*) is accepted, then the determination of the duration of the maintenance of the gross body (*audārika-śarīra*) without solid food (*kāvalikāhāra*) is established for that very reason; since the scriptures prohibit the maintenance of the gross body without food for a period exceeding the specifically fixed time of one year and so forth for the first Tīrthaṅkaras and others.

It was stated that there is no possibility of a reason for dividing the Sūtras to establish the superiority of that specific duration of fasting; however, that too is incorrect. For the very long-term endurance of the Blessed One’s body itself serves as the reason for dividing the Sūtras, since it was just explained that the continued existence of his body is impossible without the food under discussion.

Furthermore, regarding the threefold conceptualization—such as whether a Kevalin eating solid food does so out of hunger, and so forth—and the subsequent proclamation of faults therein, that too is merely the prattle of the naked one (Digambara), whose light of wisdom has been utterly eclipsed by a mass of extreme darkness. For, in the first alternative, you have raised the objection that the Lord, if eating out of hunger, would incur the fault of being subject to suffering; yet that is not a fault at all.

Because it is experienced as unpleasant (*asātānubhavatvāt*), and because that which arises from karma to be experienced as such can exist until the final moment of the state of incapacity (*ayogyavasthā*); for there is no way to prevent the arising of an effect when its causes are complete, otherwise it would be impossible for that [karma] to have that [effect] as its cause. Nor should it be argued that the karma to be experienced as unpleasant does not produce its own effect because it is like the configuration of a burnt rope; for by that same logic, it would follow that the karma to be experienced as pleasant (*sātāvedanīya*) also fails to produce its own effect, which would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the experience of pleasure (*sukhānubhava*) is absent in the Blessed One.

Just as the maintenance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth occurs through the arising of life-span-determining karma (*āyuṣka-karma*), which is comparable to the form of a burnt rope, so too should the present case be accepted; for there is no difference [between the two].

Furthermore, since the eleven types of afflictions (*pariṣaha*), such as hunger and so forth—which are of the nature of suffering—are established as existing in a *kevalin* based on the Sūtra stating "the Jina has eleven," how could hunger, being of the nature of suffering, not be established there?

Prabhācandra, however, while reflecting upon two preceding and subsequent sūtras—namely, "fourteen for the chadmastha-vītarāga" and "all for the bādara-saṃparāya"—which are devoted to positive injunctions (*vidhi*), sought to establish the intermediate sūtra, "eleven for the jina," as being focused on negation (*niṣedha*). To this end, he disregarded the well-known and possible meaning of the word "eleven" (*ekādaśa*) as being "ten plus one," and instead interpreted even the scriptural authority (*āgama*) "eleven for the jina" as being intended to negate the eleven afflictions such as hunger (*kṣudh*) and so forth.

One must proceed [in this manner]. Since the etymological derivation is "that which exceeds ten by one is eleven," he who imagines such a meaning [as you have] certainly has never heard—even though it is known to those learned in all the arts—the principle that, where possible, those words well-known in common usage should be understood in the Sūtras to have precisely those same meanings, rather than having their meaning imagined through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and the like, or being subjected to technical redefinition (*paribhāṣā*).

Indeed, the meaning of the word *ekādhikadaśa* (eleven) as its own essential form is well-known; nor is it impossible, for the eleven afflictions (*parīṣaha*) that arise from the maturation of karmic sensations (*vedanīya*) are possible therein. If it is asked: "Since the meaning characterized by the negation of eleven is also well-known, how can this [meaning] be attributed to it?"—then listen, all you venerable members of the assembly, with your ears attentive:
"If the meaning of the word 'eleven' is thus renowned anywhere... (Verse 430)

Nor is that possible, because the principle regarding the arising of what is to be experienced (*vedanīya*) and so forth has already been demonstrated. Furthermore, in the expression "eleven" (*ekādaśa*), the negative particle (*nañ*) must be connected either with the word "ten" (*daśa*) as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) or as a simple negation (*prasajya*). If it were an exclusion, then "eleven" would refer to nine and so forth which are similar to ten, or eleven and so forth would be the denotations of the word "ten.

Furthermore, if one were to analyze the compound as *ekena adhikā daśa* ("ten plus one"), it would follow that twelve or more hardships (*parīṣaha*) are prescribed therein; how then could this sūtra be intended to exclude eleven hardships? If such an application [of the meaning] were to occur, then the compound *adaśa* would not be possible, because compounds are prohibited in that context.

Even granting this, if the word *adaśa* were to convey merely the negation of ten, what kind of connection could there be between the negation of ten and the word "one" in the phrase "more than one" (*ekena adhikā adaśa*)? Thus, this poor fellow—his mind disordered by his dogmatic attachment to his own view—mocks himself with such feeble reeds as the *kāśa* and *kuśa* grass.

Furthermore, while expressing his agreement with the doubt raised by himself in the commentary on the *Sūtra* regarding the "Eleventh Victor," Vidyānanda declared this: "In that case, hunger and the like did not exist even in the Lord of Victors (*jinendra*). For although the karma of feeling (*vedanīya*) exists there, being devoid of delusion (*moha*), it lacks the capacity to produce them, just as in the case of a man who is well-known to be in a state of indifference. This is true; however, they are designated there only figuratively (*upacāreṇa*)."

Just as there is the designation "meditation" (*dhyāna*) even for one who has no mind and directly perceives all objects, despite the absence of the cessation of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛttinirodha*), if it is asked what the basis for that metaphorical designation is, [the answer is]: "The presence of the eleven factors of that causal complex which are to be experienced. This very point, while imparting a slight joy to the hearts of the connoisseurs, reveals that such a designation is indeed not literal.

For indeed, the "totality" (*sāmagrī*) referred to is the presence of the eleven types of karma to be experienced; thus, when [the opponent] points out this "totality" as the basis for the metaphorical designation of the eleven types of pain in the *kevalin*, what is intended is precisely that totality characterized by *vedanīya* karma augmented by *mohanīya* karma. And that [definition] cannot withstand scrutiny. For even in the absence of augmentation by *mohanīya* karma, it is logically possible for *vedanīya* karma to perform its own function in the *kevalin*, just as the *nāma*-karma and other such karmas do.

Otherwise, even the non-action (*akarma*) of the founders of other sects (*tīrthakara*) would not possess the superior efficacy for accomplishing their own goals, such as the establishment of a religious order. Thus, the figurative explanation (*upacāra-vacana*) is untenable, because it has been established that the afflictions (*parīṣaha*) arising from their own causes exist in the *kevalin* in a primary sense (*mukhya-vṛtti*). This will be demonstrated further below. By this, Sarvārthasiddhi is also refuted, who provides a figurative interpretation here.

As for the alternative position he proposed—that one must supply the phrase "the afflictions do not exist" in each case regarding the Jinas—that too is not subtle. For an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) should be made only when the subject matter at hand is either unestablished or impossible, and not otherwise.

And it has already been stated that such a thing does not exist here [in the case of a Kevalin]. Regarding the second alternative—that the maintenance of the body is otherwise inexplicable—it may be argued that the possession of infinite power (*anantavīryatva*), which is said to be the cause for the maintenance of the body even in the absence of the food under discussion, exists indeed even during the state of being a non-omniscient (*chadmastha*), since immeasurable strength is heard of in that state. However, even so, in that state, it is not that [power] alone which is the cause for the maintenance of the body in the absence of the food under discussion.

Otherwise, it would be inconsistent for the Blessed One—who was exerting himself in ascetic practices such as fasting for the sake of the destruction of karma—to have consumed food and other sustenance as a means for maintaining life. Nor can it be asserted that while his [digestive capacity] was *kṣāyopaśamika* during the state of being a non-omniscient (*chadmastha*), it became *kṣāyika* in the state of omniscience (*kevalyavasthā*), and thus served as the basis for the maintenance of the body even in that state of omniscience without the need for specific food.

Even though there is the presence of *kṣāyika* (destructive) energy (*vīrya*), there is no contradiction in [the Kevalin] taking the food under discussion, just as sitting and other such actions exist for the sake of maintaining the body. Nor is it unproven that even sitting and so forth are for the purpose of maintaining the body; for we hear in scripture that during the interval between the various stages of the *samudghāta*, the Kevalin returns the seats, stools, and other items [to their owners]. And it is not possible to return those items without having accepted them. As for the third alternative—that he eats by his very nature—that is refuted simply because it is not admitted.
And as for this which is said:

Does the Jina, the Kevalin, eat merely for the sake of maintaining the body? Or so that his knowledge and other qualities may not perish? Or perhaps to alleviate hunger? Or to ensure that his lifespan is not exhausted prematurely? Is it for the sake of preserving the state of liberation from decay? Or to destroy an intense craving for flavors? Or is it to show favor to the world? [433]

Thus, regarding this, the first position—that [the Blessed One eats] for the sake of maintaining the body—is not accepted. For the Blessed One does not eat with the intention, "May nourishment arise in my body," because he is free from passion (*vītarāga*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that he, like an ordinary person, would possess passion. Nor is the second position—that [he eats] so that his knowledge and other qualities may not diminish—accepted. This is because the imperishability of his knowledge and other qualities is established precisely due to the absence of any cause for their diminution.

For the cause of the exhaustion of knowledge and so forth is karma such as the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*). Since that [karma] does not exist in the Blessed One, whose obscurations have been entirely destroyed, how could there even be a suspicion of the exhaustion of knowledge and so forth? Therefore, the Blessed One does not eat even for the purpose of protecting against their exhaustion. However, the third position—that he eats for the sake of alleviating hunger—is indeed accepted.

Furthermore, the refutation that is exposed here by the ignorant—that because suffering is impossible in the Blessed One due to his state of infinite bliss, eating there for the sake of counteracting the sensation of hunger is untenable—is utterly incoherent. This is because infinite bliss itself is not established for a *kevalin* residing in existence (*bhavastha*); rather, since both pleasant and unpleasant karma (*sātāsātavedanīyakarman*) are possible, it is well known that even there, pleasure is accompanied by some degree of suffering.

The fourth position—that [the Bodhisattva] does not eat for the sake of protecting the exhaustion of his lifespan when Nirvana has not yet been achieved—is also not accepted; for those who possess the final and supreme [state], their lifespan is simply non-reversible. Since it is impossible for a non-reversible lifespan to undergo exhaustion except upon the completion of its natural duration, he does not eat even for the sake of protecting the exhaustion of his lifespan. Furthermore, the fifth position—that he eats to destroy intense craving for flavors—is likewise not admitted.

Since even a mere craving for flavor is impossible in the Blessed One who is free from delusion, the sixth position—that He eats in order to favor the world—is also not accepted. Indeed, the Blessed One does not consume food preceded by the intention, "I shall favor the world. However, in the case of a common *kevalin*, there is an activity caused by his own inherent nature (*svabhāva*), which is produced by his own karma and not by external factors, for the purpose of favoring the world.

For the Tīrthaṅkara, however, the name "Tīrthaṅkara" is produced by the power of the arising of *tīrthakṛt-nāma-karma*, which is based on his inherent nature (*svābhāvya*). As the venerable Umāsvāti Vācaka said: "That karma which is declared to have the result of establishing the *tīrtha* is called *tīrthakara-nāma*. Due to its arising, even though the Arhat has already accomplished his purpose, he establishes the *tīrtha*. Just as the sun illuminates the world solely through its own inherent nature, so too does the Tīrthaṅkara proceed to establish the *tīrtha*."

For that Blessed One, during the forenoon and the afternoon—up until three-quarters of a watch remains—he remains seated upon the lion throne and other seats precisely at the time for teaching the Dharma. As for the remainder of the day, he spends it as he pleases in a divine abode named Devacchandaka.

And there, having recognized that the food brought by the Gaṇadharas, gods, and others was purified of all defects, he accepts it when the sensation of hunger arises. Those with the eye of flesh see the food placed upon his sprout-like hands, but they do not see how he eats; for the eating and moving of an omniscient one is beyond the range of the eye of flesh.

Furthermore, regarding what Prabhācandra, following [others], has said: "For what purpose did the Blessed One stay in Devacchandaka? Was it for the sake of achieving meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) by avoiding mental distraction; or for the sake of remaining at ease due to an inability to endure cessation (*nirodha*); or for the sake of performing secret activities?"—of these, the first position is untenable. This is because, due to the state of being without mind (*amanaska*), mental distraction is impossible for the Blessed One; rather, the designation "meditation" there is merely figurative, based on the presence of the cessation of yoga. The second position is also illogical.

Because it is impossible for one of infinite power to be incapable of cessation; and because for one endowed with infinite bliss there is not even a trace of suffering, the expression "according to his pleasure" would likewise be untenable. Furthermore, a secret act must be either blameworthy or blameless. It cannot be blameworthy, because for one whose defects have been entirely destroyed, the performance of a blameworthy act is a contradiction; for such a person is free from delusion, and [blameworthy acts] are prohibited for the Blessed One. Or, if they were not prohibited, why would he go to a secluded place to eat?

[Is this] out of fear of [wrong] views, fear of beggars, or because it is an improper practice? Among these, the first alternative is untenable, because the Blessed One is beyond the sphere of the fault of [wrong] views. Moreover:
"It neutralizes leprosy, wears away fever, uproots urinary stones, withers consumption, destroys wasting disease, and crushes boils in an instant."
O wise ones, it is truly remarkable that even when the names of those [beings] are somehow remembered, a great fear of their gaze arises in the continuum of living beings! (434)

Regarding the second alternative, however, the Blessed One has demonstrated a great degree of humility. Indeed, it is not fitting for a Great Being to leave behind disciples who are clinging to his heels and are tormented by hunger, and go off alone to eat like a father leaving his sons; rather, it is better to conceive of that situation as the performance of what is appropriate.

It is like the conceptualization of serving women and so forth. Furthermore, the exhaustion of karmas—whether those previously acquired or those acquired at the time of experience—is prescribed for the Arhats therein. If it refers to those previously acquired, are they destructive (*ghāti*) or non-destructive (*aghāti*)? They cannot be the destructive ones, because those have already been exhausted prior [to that state]. Nor can they be the non-destructive ones, because those will be exhausted in due course; moreover, this [state] is capable of utterly burning away the mass of fuel that is karma by means of the fire of constant white meditation (*śukladhyāna*).

Indeed, it is not logical to maintain that the fire of the Lord’s white meditation (*śukladhyāna*) blazes only in the *devacchandaka* (the bedchamber) and not in the assembly hall (*samavasaraṇa*) and other places; for if he were situated there [in the assembly hall], it would follow that he was in another state of meditation. Furthermore, how could there be the exhaustion of karma acquired at the time of eating? If you say it is through confession (*pratikramaṇa*), let it be so; however, the faultlessness of the Lord remains difficult to establish. One who performs confession is not faultless, just as we and others perform confession, and yet the Lord does so as well.

For *pratikramaṇa* is indeed the removal of committed faults; how could one who performs it be faultless? Or, if he does not perform it, how could he remove the fault produced by the act of eating? Indeed, it is a great marvel that even by the mere mention of food, a virtuous person (*sādhu*)—though previously heedful—becomes heedless, whereas an Arhat does not become so even while eating. Furthermore, if he were possessed of faults, he would have fallen from the spiritual stages (*śreṇi*) and thus would not be entitled to receive morsels of food.

And as for the claim that he was not seen by those with fleshy eyes while eating, what is the reason for this? Is it because he was shrouded by a dense mass of darkness, or because his limbs were concealed by a screen or similar object, or because he had rendered himself invisible through a special power (*vidyā*), or because of some extraordinary greatness (*māhātmya*) surpassing that of other men? Among these, the first alternative is untenable; for by the radiance of his body, the veil of darkness would have been eradicated root and branch. Furthermore, how could alms be given to him if his limbs were covered by a screen or the like?

Furthermore, if one accepts that he possesses a specific type of supernatural knowledge (*vidyā*), there is a contradiction with his state of being a *nirgrantha* (Jaina monk), as would be the case for a *vidyādhara* or similar beings. If it is claimed that he possesses some particular excellence of greatness surpassing other people—by virtue of which he is not seen while eating—then surely an excellence surpassing other people should be accepted as consisting solely in the absence of hunger, since that alone is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). All of this is the mere prattle of this shameless man, whose intellect is enslaved by beginningless false predispositions (*mithyāvāsanā*).

For instance: as for the three positions raised and refuted—beginning with "for the sake of accomplishing meditative absorption by avoiding mental distraction"—in that regard, you have merely experienced the parching of your throat by refuting the first and third positions, because you are criticizing what has not been accepted [by us]. However, this second position—that "the Blessed One goes to Devacchandaka for the sake of remaining at ease due to an inability to endure cessation"—is indeed accepted.

Furthermore, as for the objection raised there—that it is impossible for Anantavīrya (the One of Infinite Prowess) to be incapable of cessation—that is untenable. For "infinitude of prowess" is not established in any self whatsoever; rather, it is taught in the supreme scripture (*paramāgama*) that the divisions of prowess are innumerable. Or, even if the Blessed One were somehow possessed of infinite prowess, nevertheless, by virtue of that very majesty, there can be no depletion of his power.

As for the slight suffering that arises from the exertion of the playful eloquence of speech—which occurs during the occasion of teaching the Dharma and is produced by the onset of fatigue—that cannot be prevented; therefore, we see it as logical that the Blessed One goes to Devacchandaka in order to allay it. Furthermore, as for what was stated—that because he is endowed with infinite bliss and lacks even a trace of suffering, the expression "as he pleases" (yathāsukham) is also difficult to justify—that too is untenable.

It has already been stated that the state of being endowed with infinite suffering is not yet established even today in the case of the Blessed One. Furthermore, regarding what was said—"The reason why he is not seen by those with fleshy eyes while he is eating is what? Is it because he is covered by a thick veil of darkness? and so forth—therein, the first three alternatives are refuted simply because they are not accepted.

The fourth alternative is accepted: that the cause for not seeing his eating is a specific greatness (*māhātmyaviśeṣa*) that surpasses that of other people. Regarding this, the objection was raised: "Surely, one should admit a superiority in the absence of hunger (*kṣudabhāvātiśaya*) for him, since that alone is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that regard, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*). For instance, the valid cognition—whether it be scripture (*āgama*) or something else—would have to concern the absence of hunger. It cannot, first of all, be scripture.

Because there is no scripture that establishes the absence of hunger in one who possesses both yoga and omniscience (sayogakevalin) as if it were an established fact. Furthermore, the absence of hunger could not be known through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) than the non-perception of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*). It cannot first be known from the non-perception of its own nature; for the non-perception of the nature of an entity that is remote (*viprakṛṣṭa*) is untenable in the case of an omniscient being, since such non-perception is defined as the perception of another object that is associated within a single act of cognition. Nor could its negation arise from anything else, whether that thing were being affirmed or denied.

[473] If [pleasure] were being enjoined, then it would have to be something that opposes hunger; for the injunction of what is not opposed does not establish [the desired result]. Yet, no opposition to hunger is perceived in the *kevalin* (the one possessed of pure knowledge). Nor is it appropriate to assert that the qualities such as knowledge themselves are what oppose hunger therein; for is it the mere presence of knowledge and so forth that opposes hunger, or a specific variety thereof?

If [the opponent maintains] that [hunger] belongs to the mere possessor of knowledge and so forth, then as the qualities such as knowledge increase, there ought to be a corresponding gradation in the diminution of hunger, just as darkness diminishes as light increases. But this is not the case; for it is not observed that hunger increases when knowledge and so forth are deficient in children and others, nor that hunger decreases in proportion to the increase of knowledge and so forth from that point onward. Therefore, hunger is not in contradiction with the mere possession of knowledge and the like.

Now, it might be argued that only those qualities such as knowledge belonging to a *kevalin* (an omniscient being) which have reached the ultimate limit of excellence are opposed by hunger; but this is not so, because it is impossible to establish this. Indeed, it cannot be established by one of limited vision (*arvāgdṛś*) that the knowledge and other attributes of a *kevalin* oppose hunger, because these [attributes] are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). Furthermore, the cognition of opposition occurs when the absence of one thing follows from the presence of another whose causes are complete—just as the presence of fire results in the absence of the sensation of cold—but this is difficult to maintain in the present case.

Since it is untenable to maintain that the qualities of an omniscient being (*kevalin*) are beyond the senses based on the perception that "hunger does not exist in his presence," the absence of hunger there cannot be established through some [quality] that is being positively enjoined. Furthermore, the entity being negated must be either the effect, the cause, or the pervader of that hunger. If it were the effect, then its cessation would only imply the cessation of a hunger capable of producing itself, but not its absolute absence.

Because there is no contradiction in the existence of a mere cause even in the absence of its effect, a cause, when it ceases, causes its effect to cease—just as fire [causes] smoke to cease. Or, a pervader, when it ceases, causes the pervaded to cease—just as a tree [ceasing causes] the *śiṃśapā* tree to cease. However, in this case, there is no cessation of any cause or pervader of hunger. Nor is there an absence of hunger due to the absence of the deluding karma (*mohanīya*), because it is impossible for that [hunger] to be its effect or to have it as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Hunger is not an effect of deluding karma (*mohanīya*), because it arises from feeling-producing karma (*vedanīya*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural tradition which states that [the remaining karmas] are "residues of feeling-producing karma. [Objection: There is no contradiction. We do not intend to deny that feeling-producing karma is the cause of hunger; rather, we maintain that deluding karma also pervades it as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). Furthermore, the production of an effect in the absence of its cooperative causes has never been observed.

If it is argued that a sprout does not indeed arise from the contact of seed, water, wind, and sunlight in the absence of earth, we say: it is not so; for the status of delusion (*mohanīya*) as a cooperative cause is unestablished.

Indeed, it is not proper to postulate anything as a concomitant cause merely out of conformity with one's own subjective intention; rather, that whose positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with respect to an effect is followed by that effect [is the cause]. And in this case, hunger has never been ascertained anywhere as following the absence of deluding karma (*mohanīya*). [Objection: But surely, such ascertainment will occur among the perfected beings (*siddhas*). [Reply: Not so, because of doubt. For, regarding the perfected beings, one might wonder: is it because of the absence of feeling-producing karma (*vedanīya*) that hunger does not occur, or is it because of the absence of deluding karma?

If it is argued that the absence of hunger in a *kevalin* (omniscient being) still existing in *bhava* (embodied existence) is certain to be caused by the absence of *mohanīya* (deluding karma), because *vedanīya* (feeling-producing karma) is present there—[we reply: no, because the very existence of hunger therein remains a subject of dispute even now. [Objection: In that case, just like *mohanīya*, *vedanīya* would not be the cause of hunger. [Reply: Not so; for its status as the cause of hunger is accepted by both parties. Furthermore, hunger does not have the nature of *mohanīya*, because [if it did] it would follow that it could be removed by the cultivation of its antidote (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*).

For that which has delusion (*moha*) as its intrinsic nature is removed by the cultivation of its antidote (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*), just as anger and the like are removed by the cultivation of patience and so forth. And since hunger is asserted by [the opponent] to have delusion as its intrinsic nature, then the treatise would have taught the cultivation of the antidote alone for the sake of counteracting the sensation of hunger. However, the seeking of alms-food (*piṇḍeṣaṇā*) is not primarily a defilement (*kleśa*), nor does it cause the obstruction of meditation or study. Furthermore, because hunger is equal to the affliction of cold and heat, it does not have delusion as its intrinsic nature.

Otherwise, even that sublation would possess the nature of delusion. [Objection: But surely, if hunger were to arise in the Blessed One, there would be a contradiction with his omniscience and other qualities, because—as in our own case—his knowledge, vision, and physical activity would be impaired by the onset of hunger. [Response: That is incorrect; for even when hunger arises after the destruction of the *jñānāvaraṇa* (knowledge-obscuring karma) and other karmas, it is impossible for those [karmas] to have been destroyed [if hunger still persists].

For that [decrease] is indeed dependent upon the emergence of karma such as the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*); therefore, in those like us, a superior degree of that decrease is logical due to the superior degree of its emergence. But in the Blessed One, because of the removal of all such obscurations without exception, there is no loss of knowledge and so forth even when hunger exists. For smoke does not arise when fire is absent, even if fuel is present. Thus, since it is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), the reason proving the absence of hunger is unestablished (*asiddha*). And so, how can there be a prohibition of eating?

This is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes [the fact of] eating: "In the Kevalin who is the subject of dispute, there is at some time the act of eating solid food (*kavalāhāra*), because the complete cause is present. Whatever has its complete cause present exists there, just as a sprout exists in a certain place. And such an act of eating solid food exists at some time in the Kevalin who is the subject of dispute.

Therefore, it exists there. Nor is the reason unestablished here; for the cause of solid food (kavalāhāra) is twofold: external and internal. Among these, the external consists of fasting and so forth, which certainly exists, and regarding this, no one disputes. The internal is characterized by the emergence of the *paryāpti*, the *vedya*, the *taijasa*, and long life (*dīrghāyuṣṭva*). That too certainly exists, because that which brings about the formation of the body, sense organs, and so on, is the specific karma called *paryāpti*.

The *vedya* (feeling-producing) karma is that which brings about pleasure and pain, known by the name *vedanīya*. The *taijasa* (fiery) karma is that which has the nature of internal heat, such as the digestion of consumed food, and is the cause of the fiery body (*taijasa-śarīra*). The *āyuṣka* (life-span) karma is the cause of long life and prolonged existence. From the rise (*udaya*) of these [karmas], the sensation of hunger arises. And this [sensation] exists in the Blessed One; furthermore, it is the cause for eating. As Śākaṭāyana said: "And there is eating by the Kevalins, possessing all its causes, just as there was previously before [attaining] omniscience."

"The cause [of hunger] is the manifestation (*udaya*) of the *paryāpti*, *vedanīya*, *taijasa*, and long-life (*dīrghāyuṣka*) [karmas]. (1) As for what Prabhācandra states—that the completeness of the causes of hunger is unproven (*asiddha*): indeed, it is only when the *vedanīya* and other karmas are accompanied by the *mohanīya* karma that they possess the full capacity to produce effects such as hunger, and not otherwise; for [otherwise] there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Just as an army is powerless when its commander has fallen, so too are the non-destructive (*aghāti*) karmas when their [power] is destroyed by delusion (*moha*).

Just as poison, once rendered non-toxic by a mantra, is unable to cause burning, fainting, or other such effects even when consumed, so too are the karmas of feeling (*vedya*) and the like, when their companion—delusion (*moha*)—has been utterly consumed by the fire of pure meditation (*śukladhyāna*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The Blessed One has no hunger, because the delusion that causes it is absent. Wherever there is an absence of the cause for something, the effect does not occur there, just as there is no smoke in a place devoid of fire. And since delusion is absent in the Arhat, [there is no hunger]. This, however, is an unconsidered statement.

For there is no contradiction in the karma of feeling (*vedanīya*) and so forth performing its own function—even when deprived of the assistance of deluding (*mohanīya*) karma—just as this is the case with the karma of name (*nāma*) and so forth. Otherwise, even the karma of name and so forth would not possess the skill to perform its own functions, such as the propagation of the *tīrtha*, in the case of a Kevalin. Now, one might argue that in the case of the name-karma and others, it is logical for pure (*śuddha*) sub-types to produce their effects because their capacity remains unobstructed therein. But is this not contradicted by the fact that the scriptures establish the arising of fruition (*vipākodaya*) for inauspicious sub-types, such as unpleasant feeling (*asātavedya*), within the Blessed One?

In the second case, however, there is no harm for us at all; for even when a certain portion of the intensity (*anubhāga*) is destroyed, it is logically consistent that unwholesome dispositions (*prakṛti*), such as those of unpleasant sensation (*asātā*) and so forth, will perform their own functions, since their capacity remains unobstructed.

If it is maintained that for those of inauspicious nature (*aśubhaprakṛti*), because their capacity is obstructed when a portion of their intensity (*anubhāga*) is destroyed, they do not perform their own function; then, since the *asthira* (unstable) name-karma is of an inauspicious nature, its capacity would likewise not be operative due to the existence of the destruction of a portion of its intensity. Consequently, the limbs of the Blessed One, such as his hands and feet, would be entirely stable; thus, even in the stage of the *sayogin* (the embodied liberated soul), the Blessed One would be devoid of activity, just as in the stage of the *ayogin*.

And thus, how could there be the establishment of religious systems? For this naked one (the Digambara), who desires gain, the very root of his position has been destroyed. By this, it is stated that the qualification of the reason just presented—namely, "because of the absence of delusion regarding its cause"—is unestablished (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*), since delusion is not proven to be the cause of hunger.

Because it has been established that even in the absence of those [other karmas], hunger is possible in the state of liberation (*kevalyavasthā*). Furthermore, this same author states: "And this hunger is not the effect of the *vedanīya* karma alone, independent of the *mohanīya* karma, such that it would occur even when delusion (*moha*) is completely destroyed. For hunger is not the effect of this *vedanīya* karma independent of the *mohanīya*; because it is a desire, like the desire for sexual pleasure (*riraṃsā*). Hunger is the desire to eat; how then could that be the effect of the *vedanīya* alone?"

Otherwise, even the desire for sexual pleasure (*riraṃsā*)—the wish to sport in wombs and so forth—would have to be the effect of that [Lord] alone. And in that case, because there would be the undesirable consequence of engaging in material food, women, and the like, he would not be distinguished from [ordinary] beings. Just as the desire for sexual pleasure ceases through the cultivation of its opposite, so too does the desire to eat. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: "The longing for food ceases through the cultivation of its opposite, because it is a longing, just like the longing for women and so forth. All of that, however, is false.

The argument that hunger is not the effect of *vedanīya* karma for one who is independent of *mohanīya* karma involves the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). If it is objected: "In that case, it would follow that even the Blessed One possesses *mohanīya* karma, because he possesses hunger," we reply: No. Because the existence of hunger is unestablished in his case. For hunger is the desire to eat, consisting of a longing for food; how could such a thing exist in the Blessed One, who is free from delusion (*nirmoha*)?

If it is asked, "Well then, how is it that he eats? [the answer is: just as one speaks even without the desire to speak, or one walks even without the desire to walk. If it is objected, "In that case, how can the proclamation found here and there—that 'desire to eat' (*bubhuṣā*) exists in the *kevalin*—be considered superior? [we reply: This is due to the metaphorical attribution of the effect to the cause. For it is only when there is a specific affliction produced by the rise of *vedanīya* karma that the "desire to eat" (*bubhuṣā*), in the form of a longing for food, arises in embodied beings.

Consequently, because that specific cause—namely, the particular affliction [of the body]—is present in the Kevalin, he is conventionally designated as "hungry. By this, the "scholarship" of the Nagnāṭa (Jaina) regarding his "erudition in the arts of buffoonery," such as the claim that "the desire to sport in wombs and so forth is *riraṃsā*," should be understood as a mere mockery. As for what was stated, "because it is a form of longing," there is a contradiction of the thesis by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), since one does not experience the cessation of hunger even through the practice of counter-contemplation (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*) in a person whose digestive fire (*jātavedas*) is intensely blazing. Therefore, hunger is not an effect of deluding karma (*mohanīya*).

And these are the very arguments stated by him: "The Kevalin does not possess hunger, because he is endowed with a nature of non-delusion which is opposed to it; for whatever is endowed with a nature opposed to something else does not possess that thing—just as a certain region endowed with the nature of a hot touch does not possess a cold touch—and likewise, the Kevalin is endowed with a nature of non-delusion opposed to hunger; therefore, he does not possess hunger."

That which is of the nature of suffering cannot exist there, just as the affliction of desire and so forth [do not exist]; and hunger is of the nature of suffering. Likewise, just as there is not even a trace of suffering in the infinite bliss found among the *siddhas*, so too is there infinite bliss for the Arhat. Furthermore, when something powerful that is opposed to another exists, it prevents the arising of its opposite, just as cold is prevented in an extremely hot place; and in the case of the Kevalin, there exists the infinite bliss that is powerful and opposed to the suffering of hunger.

Whatever is opposed to its own effect and cannot be removed, even if present in its entirety, does not produce that effect. For example, in a person afflicted by a disorder of bile (pitta) and the like—which is opposed to phlegm (śleṣman) and so forth and cannot be removed—curds and other such things do not produce phlegm and the like. And the Blessed One is one whose ignorance (sudha) is opposed to the fruit of what is to be known and cannot be removed. Therefore, all those [arguments] are fallacious proofs (sādhanābhāsa), because they are tainted by defects such as being unestablished (asiddhatva) and so forth.

For instance, the first proof—that [hunger] is characterized by being endowed with a nature opposed to delusion—is unestablished in its qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*), because such opposition is unproven. Indeed, there is no bond of opposition between hunger and a nature free from delusion; for it has been established that hunger, which is caused by the arising of *vedanīya* karma, exists even in the Blessed One who is devoid of delusion. Furthermore, the proof consisting in the claim that [hunger] is of the nature of suffering is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the affliction of cold and heat.

Furthermore, O Blessed One, the affliction of cold and heat is of the nature of suffering, and it must not be claimed that even this does not occur there; for that would contradict the scripture stating, "There are eleven hardships (*parīṣaha*) for a Jina. Moreover, the third proof, called "possessing infinite bliss," is also unestablished; for that [bliss] is possible only for the perfected ones (*siddhas*) who are entirely liberated from karma, but not for an Arhat, because even there the possibility of suffering produced by non-meritorious karma (*asadvedya*) exists.

Furthermore, the fourth probans—characterized by being a powerful force opposing the suffering of hunger and consisting of infinite happiness—is unestablished (*asiddha*), because the impossibility of infinite happiness was stated by the Blessed One immediately prior [to this]. For this very reason, the fifth probans as well—the nature of which consists in being endowed with an indestructible happiness that contradicts the fruit of what is cognizable—is likewise unestablished; thus, it should be disregarded by those who possess ears. As for that which he himself set forth as a probans in the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*:

"The Kevalin does not eat, because otherwise the absence of passion and aversion and the presence of infinite energy would be inexplicable"—this argument also is not conclusive. For it is impossible that the absence of passion and aversion and the presence of infinite energy in the Kevalin are inexplicable only through the absence of eating; since there is no contradiction between those two factors—being dependent on their own respective causes—even in the absence of eating.
