For in the Kevalin, there exists the cause for the absence of passion and aversion, which is the dissolution of deluding karma (*mohanīya-karma*), and the cause for the presence of infinite vigor (*ananta-vīrya*), which is the removal of the obstructive karma to vigor (*vīryāntarāya-karma*). Here, the infinitude of vigor has been established according to the acceptance of others, because in that scripture (*āgama*) it is stated to be precisely "innumerable" (*asaṅkhyāta*). And how could even speech, movement, and so forth be possible in the Kevalin if he were asserted to be such [as finite]?

For it could indeed be argued that "the Kevalin neither speaks, nor walks, nor sits down, because otherwise the absence of passion and hatred and the presence of infinite vigor would be inexplicable. However, since this argument lacks the necessary logical necessity (*anyathānupapatti*), it is not a valid means of proof for establishing its own probandum—the absence of speech, movement, and so forth.

For instance, even in the absence of attachment and aversion, and despite the presence of infinite vigor (*anantavīrya*), speech, movement, and so forth are indeed possible in the Blessed One due to their own causes—namely, the arising of the *nāmakarma* known as "Tīrthaṅkara," which has the fruit of establishing the religious order (*tīrtha*). Otherwise, the very continuity of the religious order would be severed. If this is argued, then how could the proof you yourself have presented possibly be effective in establishing your own thesis, namely the negation of the omniscient one’s eating?

Moreover, it is indeed possible to argue that even in the absence of passion and hatred, and despite the presence of infinite vigor (*anantavīrya*), the Blessed One’s consumption of solid food is logically established solely from its own cause—namely, the arising of karma to be experienced as pleasant (*sātāvedanīya-karma*), which is characterized by the production of suffering. Otherwise, there would be no remedy for the sensation of hunger. Thus, the weak arguments put forward by Anantavīrya and others regarding the proof of the omniscient one’s (*kevalin*) eating are merely fallacious.
Others as well—those who are themselves masters of an intellect radiant with sound reasoning—should also be refuted. (435)
For this reason,
[there is no debate] with those Digambaras who are not arrogant, yet whose understanding has been consumed by the fire of false pride.
How great indeed does the excessive quarreling of the Śvetāmbaras appear at every single step! || 436 ||
Whatever slight portion of reasoning has been shown here, it is primarily intended to follow the meaning of the Jina’s scriptures;
whether it is consistent with other [reasoning] or not, the elders who investigate will discern the truth. (437)

Thus, since the cause for the eating by the *kevalin* has been established, the logical reason (*hetu*)—"because the complete cause is present"—is proven. Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is entirely excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), such as delicious streams, lotuses, and the like. In this way, it is turned back from even a speck of the stain of every possible refutation.
This proof indeed establishes the enjoyment of the Kevalin. || 438 ||

Now, this inference regarding the eating of solid food by a *kevalin* is as follows: The subject of dispute is that a *kevalin* sometimes possesses solid food (*kavalāhāra*), because, while being a *kevalin*, he possesses a long-lasting bodily existence. Whatever does not possess solid food at some time does not possess a long-lasting bodily existence while being a *kevalin*, just like an atom (*paramāṇu*). And the *kevalin* who is the subject of dispute does not fail to possess a long-lasting bodily existence while being a *kevalin*; therefore, he is endowed with the aforementioned probandum (*sādhya*).

The term "subject of dispute" (*vivāda*) is employed to exclude from the class of subjects those who have eliminated [karmas] through non-yoga (*ayogika*), as well as the omniscient ones (*kevalin*) and the perfected ones (*siddha*). The qualification "at some time" (*kadā cit*) is added to the probandum (*sādhya*) to prevent the undesirable consequence that the omniscient one always possesses food. If it were stated simply as "because of having a long-lasting bodily existence," there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to one-sensed beings, gods, and hell-beings; to eliminate this, the qualification "while being omniscient" (*kevalitve sati*) is added.

However, while this very [qualification] is operative, there remains an inconclusiveness (*anaikānta*) due to the perfected ones and those in the state of non-yoga; to prohibit that, the term "long-lasting" (*dīrgha*) and so forth is adopted. And thus:
From this inference as well, the eating by the Kevalins reaches the state of proof.
Therefore, O members of the assembly, not even the slightest fault can be found here. 439.

[480] Furthermore, how could the maintenance of the body for a period of nearly ten million prior *koṭis* of years by a *sayogakevalin* (one who possesses omniscience but still has active yoga) be possible without food? If it is argued that because of his infinite power (*anantavīrya*), his maintenance occurs even without it, then by that same logic, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of his maintenance occurring even without the life-force karma (*āyuḥkarman*); thus, the body and so forth would never perish, and liberation would be rendered impossible. Or, if the maintenance of the body depends upon the life-force karma, then let it likewise depend upon food.

Because there is no distinction in the causality of both [food and non-food]. Furthermore, the body is comparable to a lamp flame or a stream of water. Just as a lamp flame does not persist when its oil is exhausted, or a stream of water does not persist without the influx of more water, so too the body cannot maintain its existence in the absence of food. Now, if food is considered a defect (*doṣa*) because fasting and other such rejections are practiced, then the claim that a *kevalin* (one who possesses omniscience) is free from defects is contradictory.

In that case, he would not be entitled to sitting and walking, because sitting and so forth are excluded by the practice of standing and other such postures; nor would he be entitled to speech, because he is observed to abide in silence. Now, if it is thought that for one who knows everything, how can there be eating while seeing meat and the like, since an obstacle (antarāya) arises—this too is the play of no small ignorance. For by the term "obstacle" is meant a specific transformation produced by the rising of obstructive karma (*antarāya-karma*).

Furthermore, there is no possibility of the occurrence of obstructive karma (*antarāyakarma*) for the Blessed One, because his destructive karmas (*ghātikarma*) have been utterly exhausted. Or, let it be granted that some obstacle might exist, fashioned by the artisan of one's own imagination; even so, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the supreme sages who possess clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhijñāna*). For they perceive the entirety of the three worlds, and yet they continue to eat.

Now, if it is argued that whenever an omniscient with clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhijñānin*) applies the mental application (*upayoga*) of clairvoyant knowledge, he perceives every single object within its range and nothing else—and thus, if he were to apply such an application at the time of eating, there would necessarily be an obstruction to that act; and that this situation cannot occur in the case of one possessing absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*), because the latter is always in a state of application (*sadopayukta*)—then, by that same logic, even his intake of food in the form of subtle, divine atoms (*divyaparamāṇu*) would be impossible.

Because of constant application, there is no interruption even when obstacles are present. Furthermore, for the Blessed One who possesses the transformation of the Great Equanimity (*mahāsāmāyika*), what room is there for an impartial inner self to consider that compassion is impaired when he sees meat and the like, even while eating? Now, if it is argued that upon eating, the attainment of flavor on the tongue entails an association with the atoms of sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) for the Kevalin;

That should not be said; for sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) does not arise merely through the connection between the sense organ and its object. Rather, it arises when there is both that connection and the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the sensory cognition-obscuring karma (*matijñānāvaraṇa*). And since this [subsidence-cum-destruction] does not exist in the *kevalin* (the one possessing omniscience) whose obscurations are entirely destroyed, there is no consequence of such cognition for him.

Otherwise, even when the auditory and other senses were connected with the sound of divine musical instruments, the forms of the *gaṇadharas* and other deities, the fragrance of perfumed flowers, incense, and ointments, or the touch of the lion-throne, sensory cognition would follow as a consequence. And thus:
This mouthful of food, agitated by longing, is unable to leave one who knows all things.
Why then do the Jain ascetics proclaim this woman as virtuous, even though she is contradictory? || 440 ||

The mental enumerations of Vyomakeśa and others, which belong to other systems, are scattered; the omniscience of the Arhat has been established through the power of subtle logic. Those wretched Kṣapaṇakas who deny his enjoyment [of worldly objects] have been somewhat instructed by means of various distinctions and subdivisions; therefore, direct perception is proven here. (441)
May that glorious one, the conqueror of the Lord of the Gods, who observes excellent vows and is known as Suvrata, protect us eternally—
he whose footstool is constantly rubbed by the tips of the edges of the clearly visible crowns of the gods in the Āmravana grove.
In his lovely body, there exists a tranquil splendor that has fully matured even as he performs his desire for the rescue of people fallen into the salt-water ocean of saṃsāra. 442.
The mountain peaks, high as the earth itself, were falling away; the Lord of Serpents was visible;
the surface of the earth was being split by the elephants of the quarters as they perished; and the great ocean was surging in agitation.
May that heroic Jina be victorious, by whom, through the mere friction of his left thumb, this world was shaken like Mount Meru with a "jhaḍ" sound, and thus became as it is.
In this world, the wise, filled with joy, practice a collection of excellent treatises that accomplishes proficiency in the art of scrutinizing through rigorous reasoning.

May those illustrious teachers, the venerable Municaṇḍrasūris, who are like a boat for crossing the ocean of the nectar of established tenets, and whose compositions are likewise [rafts], be forever gracious toward us. (444)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Determination of the Nature of the Primary and Subsequent Divisions of Direct Perception," in the *Syādvādaratnākara*, an Ornament Illuminating the Reality of the Means of Cognition and the Methods of Inquiry, composed by the venerable Devācārya—who subsists on the honey from the lotus feet of the illustrious Municaṃdrasūri, whose intellect is like a powerful press for crushing sugarcane and who has cast aside the crest-jewels of all rival monastic scholars—within the *Śrīlalitavistara*. 2.
